name: Farley, Robert E.
text: In the Utah War call-up of 1857 he and Parson served as privates in the same platoon of a Weber District militia company mustered at Ogden, he from October 20 and Parson from November 9 (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, Utah State Archives), and in July 1860 they were next-door neighbors near Ogden, both tanners (1860 U.S. census, Weber County, p. 155). Called by name to settle his affairs and move to South Weber with John Parson (Revelation No. 46, Weber, February 12, 1861; Spirit Prevails, pp. 60–61). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Robert Farley”). The Morrisites' bugler: he kept sounding the bugle under fire as the fort surrendered on June 15, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137). He moved from Utah to Omaha in 1864 and to Wisner, Nebraska, in 1867, and joined the RLDS Church in 1870 (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2); a descendant's family tradition of a Farley who moved to Nebraska and joined the RLDS Church fits him (see note 9). name: Bar, Labrach
text: Johann Lebrecht Bar (John L. Bear, 1838–1919), born at Affoltern, Canton Zürich, emigrated in 1860 on the Underwriter , where Mark H. Forscutt led the singing at his marriage to Susanna Sidler (Baer autobiography, MS 10240, p. 16). He signed the oath of the Soldiers of Israel in May 1862, and on June 13 a cannon ball killed Susanna and their infant son; their daughter Barbara survived (Young, Contributor 11, 1890, p. 284; MS 10240, pp. 25–26; Saints’ Herald 34, 1887, p. 207). He went to Soda Springs in 1863, joined the Reorganized Church in 1869 (in a letter of 1870 he gives the child killed with his wife as 18 weeks old and reports a branch of seven at Soda Springs; Saints’ Herald 17, 1870, pp. 242–43), served it on a mission to Switzerland in 1880–82, and died at Independence in 1919 (MS 10240, p. 89).

name: Eardley, John R.
text: John R. Eardley, an Englishman called to the Morrisite apostleship in September 1861, left the fort with his family during the siege and was discharged on June 16, 1862 ( Spirit Prevails , p. 142; CR 100 397). A follower of George Williams (Cainan), he lived in California and, in 1873–74, in England, then in 1882 opened the store and post office at Willow Glen, Montana, and later worked as a legislative clerk at Helena and in business at Anaconda (MS 31876; New North-West , 1882–89). He compiled Gems of Inspiration (1899), the movement’s own history.

name: Dow, Alexander Sr.
text: Alexander Dow, a tinsmith who reached Salt Lake City in 1856, joined Morris and was close to Burton at the surrender; his affidavit of April 18, 1863, on Burton’s shooting of Morris was widely printed (Anderson, pp. 133, 139, 148–49; Waite, 1866, pp. 127–28). He was spokesman of the Soda Springs company in 1863 and an early follower of Cainan, then lived at St. Louis, where the Reorganized Church would not receive him, and in 1874 was named a counselor to John Parson in California (Anderson, pp. 159, 168; MS 31876). His papers, with manuscripts of Morris’s revelations, are the Joseph Morris Papers (P11-1, Community of Christ Library Archives). In December 1876 James Bowman of Soda Springs advertised in the Reorganized Church’s paper for word of Dow, “a member of the St. Louis branch about the year 1869” ( Saints’ Herald 23, December 1, 1876, p. 734).

name: Firth, John
text: One of the six founding members of the church, April 6, 1861 (Anderson, p. 66); ordained a high priest (Spirit Prevails, p. 77; Anderson, p. 65). Revelation concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 51–52. Family Tree (FamilySearch KWVG-KDB, born 1823) places him at South Weber; his sons William H. and Arthur are also on the roll. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “John Firth”). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 33 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 9024). Price’s journal names him among the same six (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Kendell, William

On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “William Kendall”). name: Jones, John E.
text: Ordained an apostle in June 1861 (Anderson, p. 67; Spirit Prevails, p. 102). The Spirit Prevails and Gems name him among the seven sentenced in March 1863 and pardoned (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31), but the court report says the jury found him not guilty of murder; he then pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and was fined $100 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Later with James Dove and John Livingstone in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 143, 177, 180). He “surrendered during the engagement” of June 13–15, 1862, and was discharged at the fort on June 16 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). On Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862, he wore one crown on his hat, the last in a descending order that began with seven on Morris’s (W. P. Thomas, letter of that evening, MS 31876, folder 21; translation generated by Claude).

name: Klemgard, Peter C.
text: Led the armed party of about thirty that captured William Jones and his companions (Anderson, p. 99, as Klemgaard); named in the writs and the contempt citation (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20); appointed to take charge of the firearms (Spirit Prevails, pp. 527–29). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree for the deaths of the posse men and sentenced to fifteen years at hard labor, the heaviest sentence (Deseret News, April 1, 1863); Governor Harding pardoned him a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31). He later followed William W. Davies. Testifying at Walla Walla in 1881, he said that he and Davies had withdrawn from the Latter-day Saint church under Morris at Weber, that he next met Davies at Soda Springs in 1865, where there were “about sixty of us Morrisites” and the camp broke up for want of a leader, and that he then went to San Francisco, where Davies’s missionaries won him over. He lived at Davies’s camp near Walla Walla with his wife and four children from April 1870 to April 1872, and added that “the doctrine taught at the Davies camp is not like the Morrisite religion” (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). The Walla Walla Statesman reported his testimony before the referee, given over more than two days: “I have known Davis for over 16 years; I made his acquaintance first in Utah, at a place called Weber; in 1864 [so printed] Davis, myself and others withdrew from the Mormons under the leadership of Morris; I next saw D

name: Taylor, Abraham
text: ## The apostle and the siege, 1861–62 Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67). A revelation explains the death of his child (Spirit Prevails, p. 115). Hans Oakason named an Abraham Taylor among the captains of the armed companies in 1862 ( Salt Lake Herald , February 26, 1879, p. 3). ## The trial and the homestead, 1862–68 In the summer and fall of 1862 John L. Bear lodged with him in Salt Lake City, and the sheriff took Taylor’s horses (Bear, autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 30–32). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to ten years at hard labor (Deseret News, April 1, 1863), and pardoned a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31); forfeited bail, and his homestead was sold (Anderson, p. 148). J. H. Beadle wrote in 1870 that after Judge Kinney declared the absent Morrisites’ bonds forfeit, Taylor’s homestead in Salt Lake City, worth $3,000, was sold to Joseph A. Johnson, clerk of Kinney’s court, for $200, and the family, “literally forced into the street,” took refuge at Camp Douglas. In 1866, through his attorney Major Charles H. Hempstead, Taylor sued in the United States District Court, and at the October term, 1868, Judge Wilson decreed him his homestead “with rents for five years” ( Life in Utah , Philadelphia, 1870, pp. 425–27). ## Later years He bought the chest of Morris's revelations, which Hannah Banks had buried in the Bowery, and kept it f

name: Gudmundson, Gudmund
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67). An artist: Morris directed him to draw the white horse larger than in his drawing of the twelve generals, and to make the crowns for the Foreshadowing (Spirit Prevails, pp. 532, 583). Later prominent among the scattered congregations (Anderson, p. 157). Almost certainly the “Gudmanson” whom Williams in 1868 named with Dow and Davies among the “rebels”: George Thompson wrote in 1869 of “Poor Goodman Goodmunsen, poor W. W. Davis and others of the Weber House, good men,” who had been “deceived by supernatural manifestations” (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, July 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874).

name: Jacobson, Niels
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67, as Neils Jacobsen). Revelations concerning him: Spirit Prevails, p. 257 and No. 211, Weber, January 28, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, pp. 391–94). Forscutt’s diary has “Niels Jacobsen Geertzen,” “an Apostle of the new faith,” leaving the camp with a man named Jensen on January 23, 1862; he came back after five days, confessed, gave up his apostleship and was received into the quorum of priests (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). The revelation of January 28 falls within those days.

name: Harris, William
text: Called by revelation to preside over the priests of Aaron (Spirit Prevails, p. 102); directed to wear a robe and carry a rod foreshadowing Aaron's on Foreshadowing Day (Spirit Prevails, pp. 551–59). The pencil list of officers marks him Bishop. Josiah D. Price copied the declaration Harris made in the bishop’s robe on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). In April 1873 Forscutt, on a Reorganized Church mission in South Wales, met a Mrs. Eastman, “the sister of William Harris, formerly Bishop of the Morrisite Church,” whom Latter-day Saint missionaries had told that her brother was “an associate of thieves and robbers” (Forscutt, journal, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University, April 30, 1873).

name: Guhl, Soren Peter
text: Soren Peter Guhl (1821–1883), born at Horsens, Jutland, came to Utah in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 and was baptized into the Morrisite church at South Weber on August 7, 1861 (Council Bluffs register, MS 32226). Held to bail after the siege as “S. P. Guhl” ( Deseret News , June 25, 1862), he lived some years in Montana, then came to Omaha in January 1869, where he was sustained as Cainan’s first counselor and organized the Omaha and Council Bluffs congregations (Anderson, pp. 193–94; Omaha minute book, MS 31876). Sent on a mission to Denmark, he founded a congregation at Copenhagen in 1871 and that year renounced Cainan, who called him a “traitor” (Anderson, p. 204). Back at Omaha in 1874, he joined the Reorganized Church in 1875 and baptized his stepfather, Carleton Fellows, and his mother, very probably the roll’s Maren Guhl, at Council Bluffs in 1876 ( Saints’ Herald 22, 1875, p. 597; 23, 1876, p. 758). He died at Council Bluffs in 1883.

name: Magee, William
text: Named as bearer of the second rod for the Foreshadowing; its inscription begins "Behold, I am William Magee, even number two" (Spirit Prevails, p. 559). Probably William Magee (1826–1890; FamilySearch KWJD-PC3), who died at Wadsworth, Nevada; his daughter Ellen is also on the roll.

name: Park, Hugh
text: His name was inscribed on the fifth scepter: "Hugh Park … even number five" (Anderson, p. 117). The Woodruff Papers identify him as the Hugh Park named on a scepter recovered after the surrender (FamilySearch note). Son of David and Ann Brooks Park (FamilySearch LLQF-CF6, KWJ5-6FF), who settled at Mottsville in the Carson Valley, Nevada; his parents and his siblings David Jr., Martha, Ellen and Joseph Hyrum are probably the roll's other Park entries. The inscription on his rod, copied from the original on June 19, 1862, reads: “Behold! I am Hugh Park—even number five,” standing “in the stead of the fifth first born son of Adam” (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). Taken at the surrender, aged 18, born in Canada (same list). Absent when the names of those bound over were called at the March 1863 term; his recognizance was declared forfeited ( Deseret News , March 18, 1863, p. 8).

name: Banks, John
text: ## Morris’s counselor, 1861–62 Joseph Morris's counselor in the church presidency and, in Forscutt's words, the movement's orator; a member of the First Council (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 24, 51); signed letters with Morris and Richard Cook (Spirit Prevails). On May 1, 1862, he rode the black horse carrying a pair of balances, and on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, he rode as the third general (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). Named with Morris, Cook, Parson and Klemgard in the May 1862 writ over the three imprisoned dissenters (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20). ## Death, June 15, 1862 Wounded at the surrender on June 15, 1862, and died that evening in custody (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Anderson, p. 137); Eardley reports he seemed to be recovering in a wagon, then was dead within the hour, citing William Jones, who went to the wagon (Gems, p. 28). T. B. H. Stenhouse wrote in 1873 that Banks was wounded at Morris’s death “but not fatally”: “In the evening he was well enough to sit up and enjoy his pipe. Suddenly he died.” Stenhouse thought him “foully dealt with” and gave a short life: an early English convert, a former Chartist, a president of large conferences and once of the presidency of the church in Britain ( The Rocky Mountain Saints , New York, 1873, p. 600). ## Family J. H. Beadle tells, as Governor Harding’s story, that “the widow of Banks, the murdered Morrisite,” came to Harding with a Danish woman to warn him of a plot to compromi

name: Cook, Richard
text: ## Bishop of South Weber, to 1861 Bishop of the LDS South Weber Ward when Morris arrived, and the first to hear his claims there (Anderson, pp. 52, 62); then in Morris's presidency. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Richard Cook”). Josiah D. Price names him first of the six whom Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, to found his church, all made high priests (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives); a revelation of April 4 names him and John Parson as the first two called (Spirit Prevails, No. 56, pp. 78–79). Summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 28). Revelations concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 37, 39, 93, 364–67, 459–61; appointment, Spirit Prevails, p. 77. ## Kington Fort and the trials, 1862–63 On May 1, 1862, he rode the red horse with a sword before the companies, and on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, he rode as the second general (Price journal). Named in the May 1862 writ and contempt citation (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20); called out by Burton at the surrender (Gems, p. 28). At the March 1863 term the prosecution dropped the murder charge against him (nolle prosequi); he pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and was fined $100, and the $50 fine for contempt of June 1862 was remitted (Des

name: Cook, John
text: Richard Cook's brother. Met Morris near the Warm Springs and brought him to South Weber, the turning point in Morris's career (Anderson, pp. 51–52, 62; Gems, pp. 12, 16). One of the six founding members of the church, April 6, 1861 (Anderson, p. 66); ordained a high priest (Spirit Prevails, p. 77) and among the first apostles (Anderson, p. 67). Revelations concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 38, 459–61. A member of the First Council; summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 28, 51). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “John Cook”). Price’s journal also names him among the six baptized on April 6, 1861 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Parson, John
text: John Parson, a tanner living up Weber Canyon, was called by revelation to South Weber in February 1861, cut off from the LDS Church that month, and named to preside over Morris’s apostles ( Spirit Prevails , pp. 60–61, 77–79). He gave the order to raise the white flag at the surrender, was fined $100 for resisting an officer in 1863, and carried Governor Harding’s pardon to the prisoners ( Spirit Prevails , p. 7; Deseret News , April 1, 1863; Gems , p. 31). He later led the Morrisites in Nevada and California, joined the Reorganized Church in 1886, was expelled in 1890 after taking up Dr. Poulson’s “Order of Messiah,” and died near Deer Lodge on June 13, 1892 (Anderson, pp. 178–81; Saints’ Herald 39, 1892, p. 438).

name: Forscutt, Mark Hill
text: Mark Hill Forscutt (1834–1903), born at Manchester, was ordained a Morrisite apostle in June 1861 and served as Morris’s secretary and translator (Anderson, p. 67; Salt Lake Herald , February 25, 1879, p. 3). He surrendered during the siege on June 14, 1862, was discharged at the fort, and testified for the defence in 1863 (CR 100 397; Deseret News , March 25, 1863, p. 5). Baptized into the Reorganized Church in 1865, he left Utah after threats in 1866 and became a leading RLDS minister; he died at Nebraska City in 1903 ( Saints’ Herald 10, 1866, pp. 142–43; 50, 1903, p. 982). His “Sketch of Joseph Morris” (Church History Library, MS 702) is the subject of the editor’s documentary edition, in preparation.

name: Dove, James
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67); led the Nevada and California Morrisites (Anderson, ch. 13, pp. 177–87). His writings are in Watson. Fined $56.80 by the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 34). He and George Dove were absent when the names of those bound over were called at the March 1863 term, and their recognizances were declared forfeited ( Deseret News , March 18, 1863, p. 8).

name: Brown, Alonzo
text: Lived with his wife in the Kington schoolhouse, where rowdies attacked them in November 1861; named in the complaint that followed (Anderson, p. 82). Carried the white flag at the surrender on June 15, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137). Fined $56.80 by the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training; Forscutt also tells the schoolhouse incident (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 34, 38). A Morrisite account of 1891 says that John Parson took him to carry the flag when he went out to surrender to Judson Stoddard (“Massacre of Morrisites,” letter 9 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891, p. 3).

name: Anderson, Niels
text: ## Kington Fort, 1862 At the fort during the siege; later said the posse allowed too little time to surrender (Anderson, p. 114). John Codman, at Soda Springs in July 1873, took his account of the surrender from the wounded girl, now married, “and her husband, who was also present” (John Codman, The Mormon Country (New York, 1874), p. 157; see Maria Christofferson). ## Soda Springs, 1863–1926 Married Mary Christofferson (probably Christofferson, Maria), wounded by the first cannon shot of the siege, on July 30, 1863, and was among the few Morrisites who stayed at Soda Springs (Anderson, p. 162); Shupe gives the date as July 20, 1863, calls theirs the first marriage in Idaho Territory, and says he was the blacksmith at Connor's post (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Their son Abraham C. Anderson was born on February 20, 1865 (Shupe, p. 16). His son Peter, writing in 1965, says he was born in Denmark in 1835, came with his family in 1860 and pulled a handcart from Florence, Nebraska; that Lieutenant Frank Shoemaker of Connor’s command married him and Mary two months after the colony reached Soda Springs, with a dance on canvas spread on the ground; and that Shoemaker later married Mary’s sister and is buried at Blackfoot, Idaho (Peter Anderson, “The Wound That Never Healed,” Frontier Times , June–July 1965, pp. 29, 46). At Burton’s trial in February 1879, after his wife had testified for the prosecution, the defense offered to prove that he had written to Burton offeri

name: Eliason, Erick
text: Erik Eliasson (1817–1893), born in Västmanland, Sweden, was baptized a Morrisite at South Weber and discharged at Kington Fort on June 16, 1862 (MS 32226; CR 100 397). He went with the Morrisites to Soda Springs in 1863, where four of his children were born and where he joined the Reorganized Church in 1870 (Shupe, pp. 13, 29; Black, Early Members , vol. 2). By 1877 he was at Race Track in the Deer Lodge Valley, where he kept the Lord’s House until the 1883 split over William James, and he died there in 1893 (council minutes, MS 31876; Powell County , pp. 108–109). Identified by his descendant Keith Chappelow.

name: Eliason, Karen
text: Karin Caroline Anderson (1830–1902), wife of Erik Eliasson (FamilySearch LHN8-4C5). Probably the Caroline Eliason who testified at Burton’s trial in February 1879 that she had belonged to the Morrisites at Weber in 1862 and remembered the armed men arriving on the Friday morning ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 21, 1879). Shupe lists Mrs. Caroline Eliason among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). They had four sons and two daughters: Caroline (born 1861 at Farmington, Utah), Anna, Joseph, the twins Jacob and John, and Isaac, the last five born at Soda Springs. Baptized into the RLDS Church with her husband on June 9, 1870, as Caroline Eliasson (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2). In June 1880 “Carrie Eliasson”, 50, was at Soda Springs with all six children (1880 U.S. census, Oneida County, Idaho, ED 25, p. 289a), while Erik was also counted farming in the Deer Lodge Valley. When Erik took the twins to the Deer Lodge Valley, part of the family stayed at Soda Springs (Powell County: Where It All Began, pp. 108–109); Karin died there in 1902. Her obituary gives her death “at her home in Soda Springs, Idaho, March 26, 1902,” her birth in Sweden in 1830 and her coming in 1860, and says that she had been “a faithful member of the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints since 1870”; four sons and two daughters survived her ( Saints’ Herald 49, 1902, p. 343). Identified by her

name: Smith, Hans Peter
text: Called to the apostleship (Spirit Prevails, p. 412). Hans Peter Smith (1811–1868; FamilySearch KJP1-Y7Z): Family Tree records his call at Kington Fort in February 1862 as one of the Morrisite Twelve Apostles, and a later residence at Carson City, Nevada.

name: Anderson, Abelone
text: Probably Appelone Maria Andersdatter (1816–1884), wife of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch KWVH-NZM); Andersdatter is the Danish form of Anderson, so she would be listed under her own patronymic. Mother of Mary Christoffersen Anderson. She died at Soda Springs in 1884.

name: Beck, Niels R.
text: Niels Rasmussen Beck (1823–1888; FamilySearch KWJ4-LNP). Family Tree describes him as a Morrisite and records his death at Deer Lodge, Montana, in 1888. His is the earliest Morrisite land title (patent) found in the Deer Lodge Valley: 160 acres he bought from the government as a settler with the right to buy first (a “pre-emption”), paid for in cash on December 22, 1870, at $200, and patented on May 1, 1871 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0070__.167). The land office’s ledger of claims, its tract book, gives two dates for his first claim: April 1, 1865, probably when he settled on the land, and April 26, 1869, when he filed. If the year is read rightly, he was living in the valley by the spring of 1865. Lars C. Hanson filed his claim the same day, giving March 2, 1865 (Bureau of Land Management tract book, Montana, vol. 5, p. 96, township 8 north, range 9 west; images on FamilySearch, “United States, Bureau of Land Management Tract Books”). His claim file at the National Archives should confirm the dates. A “Neil A. [or R.?] Beck of Montana” sent gifts by letter and money order to William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, the first of them toward the purchase of its eighty acres, according to Swen O. Hagg’s testimony in 1881, and a list of donations filed in the same case credits “Neils R. Beck” with $4,839 between 1866 and 1878. Davies himself testified that he had received “over $1500 from Mr. Beck to pay for land,” $300 for a printing press and more

name: Christoffersen, Christian
text: Probably Christen Pedersen (1845–1895), son of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch KWJN-123): the Chris Christofferson whom Shupe lists among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He married Bertha Hansen, daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, and died at Soda Springs in 1895. A Chris Christofferson, probably he, proved up a 160-acre homestead near Soda Springs (Boise Meridian, T8S R40E, secs. 22–23 and 26), patented August 3, 1888 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-ID0120__.123). The 1880 U.S. census lists “C. Christopherson”, born in Denmark about 1846, and his wife Bertha at Soda Springs (1880 U.S. census).

name: Christoffersen, Peter
text: Peder Christophersen (1810–1891), a Danish convert who came to Utah with his family in 1859 (FamilySearch KWVH-NCY). The Church History Department's pioneer database places them in an 1859 company. A family account in a 1989 county history says the family left Denmark in 1857, that polygamy did not fit their way of life, and that for safety they joined the Morrisites who were going north (Powell County: Where It All Began, p. 111). His grandson Peter Anderson, writing in 1965, says the family emigrated in 1857 and was held at Burlington, Iowa, until 1859; that a stove they had to leave behind on the trail later turned up in the home of one of Brigham Young’s wives; and that Peter turned against the church when the daughters were pressed to become plural wives: “They never said anything about polygamy in Denmark” (Peter Anderson, “The Wound That Never Healed,” Frontier Times , June–July 1965, p. 28). The Church History Department's pioneer database records that he and his son Andrew signed a Morrisite oath in May 1862. Shupe lists him among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Father of Mary Christoffersen Anderson; he died at Soda Springs in 1891.

name: Christofferson, Andrus
text: Anders Pedersen (1841–1921), son of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch L2XW-JS2): the Andrew who signed a Morrisite oath with his father in May 1862 (Church History Department pioneer database). Shupe lists Andrew Christoffersen among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He married Christiane Marie Hansen, daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, and died at Deer Lodge, Montana, in 1921. According to the same county history, he tried mining in Idaho, then cattle at Bannack and Virginia City, and in 1874 settled in the Deer Lodge Valley, where he started a dairy (Powell County: Where It All Began, p. 111). His 160-acre homestead in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, sec. 28) was patented on November 23, 1891 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0250__.196). The 1880 U.S. census, however, lists “A. Christopherson”, born in Denmark about 1841, and his wife Katie at Soda Springs, Idaho, so the family may have moved between the two places (1880 U.S. census).

name: Christofferson, Ida
text: Ida Pedersen (1850–1924), daughter of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch L75M-CRD). Shupe lists her among the Morrisite families who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 and says she married Lieutenant Shoemaker, the first soldier married at the fort (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13); Family Tree names her husband as Francis Marion Shoemaker. She died at Sedro-Woolley, Washington, in 1924.

name: Christofferson, Maria
text: Probably Mary Anne Christoffersen (1847–1928), daughter of Peter and Abelone Christoffersen, whose chin was shattered by the first cannon shot at Kington Fort on June 13, 1862, and who later witnessed Morris’s death (Anderson, pp. 119, 140). She married Niels Anderson at Soda Springs in 1863 and lived there until her death in 1928; she told her story to John Codman in 1873 and testified at Robert T. Burton’s trial in 1879 (Codman, The Mormon Country , p. 157; Salt Lake Herald , February 21, 1879). The roll has two Marias; which entry is hers is not certain.

name: Christofferson, Matilda
text: Probably Matthia Pedersen (1840–1908), daughter of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch LHFM-68F). She married Lars Hansen, son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, so she is probably the Mrs. Matilda Hansen whom Shupe lists at Soda Springs in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). She died at Grand Forks, British Columbia, in 1908.

name: Lee, Andrew
text: Andrew Lee (1818–1863; FamilySearch 2ZS4-6YS), husband of Charlotte Lee; Family Tree says they joined the Morrisite movement together. At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to ten years at hard labor; he was also among the men tried for resisting an officer (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The Spirit Prevails and Gems name a George Lee among the seven instead (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31). Holley says Andrew Lee died before the trial and that his widow Charlotte then married a soldier, Charles Cooney (Holley, UHQ 2008), but the court report shows him alive and sentenced in March 1863; Family Tree gives his death that year.

name: Lee, Charlotte
text: Charlotte Lee (1822–1865; FamilySearch L5F4-44L). Family Tree says she and her husband, Andrew Lee, came to Utah in the James Brown company, joined the Morrisite movement and were excommunicated.

name: Hanson, Christian
text: Probably Christiane Marie Hansen (1846–1927), daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson (FamilySearch MG21-P6Q). She married Andrus (Anders) Christoffersen and lived and died in the Morrisite community at Deer Lodge, Montana. The roll has two Christian Hansons.

name: Hanson, Hans
text: Probably Hans Rasmus Hansen (1838–1911), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson (FamilySearch KF11-1MK). Shupe lists Hans Hansen among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863, along with a Mrs. Amelia Hansen (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13); Hans Rasmus married Christine Amalia Christoffersen. He died at Blackfoot, Idaho, in 1911. He may instead be the roll's second Rasmus Hanson; which man is which is not settled.

name: Hanson, Lars
text: Probably Lars Hansen (1842–1911), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, who came to Utah with the family in 1859 (FamilySearch LY9T-Z79). Shupe lists a Lars Hansen among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He married Matilda Christoffersen and died at Grand Forks, British Columbia, in 1911. The roll also has a Lars Christian Hanson. A Lars Hansen, probably he, received patents for land near Soda Springs in section 22, next to Chris Christofferson’s homestead: a 160-acre cash entry patented in 1891 and another tract in 1896 (Boise Meridian, T8S R40E; BLM General Land Office records, accessions STA-ID0020__.206 and STA-ID0090__.326). In 1880 Lars Hansen, born in Denmark about 1841, and his wife Matilda were living at Soda Springs (1880 U.S. census).

name: Cook, Ellen
text: Probably Ellen Haworth (born 1820), wife of Richard Cook (FamilySearch LCCJ-LS7, probable match). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Hellen Cook”).

name: Cook, Hannah
text: Probably Hannah Peek (1814–1895), who married Richard Cook in 1854 and died in Nevada (FamilySearch LZW3-1Q2, probable match). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Hannah Cook”).

name: Cook, Margaret
text: ## Utah and Weber, 1821–62 Margaretta Julia Greatrix (1828–1888), wife of John Cook (FamilySearch LHV7-2NX); she lived at Franktown, Nevada, in 1880 and died at Mottsville in the Carson Valley. On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Margaret Cook”). A Margaret Cook, probably she, interpreted a tongue given through Morris in a fellowship meeting at Weber on March 9, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, pp. 634–35); a Danish copy of it is among Morris’s revelations in the Niels Jensen record of the 1870s (Church History Library, MS 31876). It is one of two tongues through Morris that the book prints with an interpreter (see Teachings, Spiritual gifts). ## Carson Valley and the Reorganized Church, 1862–88 She belonged to the Morrisites until 1870 and was baptized into the RLDS Church at Sheridan, Nevada, in September 1873 (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2, s.v. “Cook, Margaretta”). Very probably the “Mary Cook” of D. R. Jones’s recollection of the RLDS Mottsville branch, organized in Carson Valley in February 1869: of the Morrisite families who came from Utah in 1862, he wrote in 1908, none ever joined the church “except one sister, Mary Cook. She was a noble Saint and had the gift of tongues.” In 1874, at a schoolhouse meeting of about thirty Morrisites and as many “Josephites” called to hear a man

name: Cook, Sarah
text: Probably Sarah Rostron (1823–1893), wife of John Cook and widow of James Cooper Holt, whose four children are on the roll (FamilySearch KWJ4-74G, probable match). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Sarah Cook”). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of her (two files, 7 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 12280).

name: Cook, Mary
text: Probably Mary Cook (1841–1904; FamilySearch LCCP-6HT, probable match). Family Tree gives her as a wife of John Cook, but the 1860 census lists her, with two small children, in Richard Cook’s household at Kaysville. Her later children, by William J. White, were born in the Carson Valley from 1863; she died at Palouse, Washington. On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Mary Cook”).

name: Brooks, Nathan
text: Probably Nathan Brooks (1793–1881), who died at South Weber (FamilySearch KWJH-PH6, probable match); his wife Elizabeth (Betty Smith) is also on the roll. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Nathan Brooks”). One of the six whom Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, to found his church, and made a high priest (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives, as “Nathan Brookes”). Aged 67, he was among the men discharged at the fort on June 16, 1862 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library).

name: Kendell, Johanna
text: Joanna Peek (1827–1900), wife of William Kendell Jr. (FamilySearch KWN2-QT3). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Joanna Kendall”).

name: Morrison, Niels
text: Named with John Trolsen and Niels Jacobson in a revelation (Spirit Prevails, p. 257). In the winter of 1864 six Morrisite apostles met with Richard Cook in Neils Morrison’s house in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 178, 180). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Nels Morrison”). Very probably the “Morrisen” who, with Jens Mikkelsen, baptized Anders and Karen Søndermark at South Weber on July 31, 1861 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library).

name: Jones, William J.
text: William J. Jones (1825–1909), a Welsh convert known as “Welsh Billy,” joined the Morrisites in April 1861 and was one of Morris’s first converts. He left the camp in the spring of 1862, was brought back by an armed party and held in chains in a log house at the fort until June 13; the writs issued over his detention brought the posse (Anderson, pp. 97–100, 107). He testified for the defense at Robert T. Burton’s trial in 1879 and farmed at South Weber until his death ( Ogden Junction , February 28, 1879, p. 4; FamilySearch K2W1-SRR, probable match).

name: Geertsen, Lars Christian
text: ## Capture and escape, 1862 Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925), born in Denmark, who reached Utah in September 1861 (FamilySearch LHN8-BJ8): the Lars Gurtsen (Lewis C. Gurtsen) who, having left the camp, was captured with William Jones and John Jensen by Peter Klemgard’s party in the spring of 1862 and held with them in a log house at the fort. Judge Kinney’s writ of habeas corpus of May 22, 1862, as printed by Richard W. Young, names the men held as “John Jensen, Louis Christian Jensen, [Lars Christian Gurtsen] and Wm. Jones”; the bracket appears to be Young’s. Young tells, from William Jones’s account, that Jones, “Gurtsen and Jensen” were seized at Kaysville by about thirty armed men under Peter Klemgaard about May 8 or 10 and held in a log house, and that Gurtsen escaped by cutting through a log ( The Contributor 11, no. 9 (July 1890): 349–50). After several days he and Jensen cut a hole through the log wall; Gurtsen escaped, and Jensen was caught and returned (Anderson, pp. 98–100, 105). William J. Jones, testifying in 1879, put it this way: “we made a hole in the wall with a pocket knife to escape; Gearson got away without his shoes” ( Ogden Junction , February 28, 1879, p. 4). The Church History Department’s biographical profile of Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925) says that he escaped and went to Salt Lake City to tell the authorities that Jones and Jensen were being held against their will, and that the posse followed. ## Salmon, Idaho, 1866–1925 A Montana county

name: Davies, William
text: William W. Davies (1833–1906), a Welsh stonemason who came to Utah in 1855, joined Morris in 1861 with his wife and was held to bail after the siege ( Deseret News , June 25, 1862). He went with a few families to Soda Springs and Montana, where on January 24, 1866, he had the vision that began his own movement, and from 1867 he led the Morrisite community near Walla Walla known as the Kingdom of Heaven, until it broke up after the lawsuit of 1880–81 (Gilbert, 1882, pp. 369–77; Anderson, pp. 157, 187–92). He died in Walla Walla County in 1906 (Find a Grave 15969383).

name: Bowman, John
text: Probably John Bowman (1824–1898), born at Kirkcaldy, Fife, who came to Utah in 1853 and married Agnes Patton, the roll’s Agnes Bowman, in 1845; he lived at Kaysville in 1870 and at South Weber in 1880 (FamilySearch KWJN-MJF, probable match). Family Tree gives his death as July 31, 1898, at Ogden; the Daughters of Utah Pioneers index gives August 31, 1897, at South Weber (DUP pioneer histories index, no. 3546). A John Bowman went from Soda Springs to Salt Lake City with George Thompson in 1865 to visit the Prophet Cainan, and later he and his wife were in James Dove’s Morrisite group in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 168, 178). Whether he is the “James Bowman” of the June 1862 prisoner list, whose wife was killed at the surrender, is not settled.

name: Bowman, Agnes
text: Probably Agnes Patton (1825–1890), born in Fife, Scotland, wife of John Bowman; she died at South Weber (FamilySearch LHFY-WFT, probable match; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 3537).

name: Moss, Joseph
text: Probably Joseph Moss (1806–1878) of Leigh, Lancashire, whose family came to Utah with the Edward Martin handcart company in 1856 and lived in Davis County in 1860 (FamilySearch KWJW-H3T, probable match). The Mosses on the roll match his household: his wife Mary (Mary Brabin) and their children Peter (Peter John), Joseph Jr., Edward, James, Hiram R. (Hyrum Ralph) and Alice; Elizabeth is not yet placed. By 1870 the family was in Nevada, and he died at Austin, Nevada, in 1878. In 1878, John R. Eardley wrote, he was returning from Austin to his son Joseph’s house when “a severe snow storm” overtook him; “he was found 2 or 3 days afterwards in a ravine, frozen stiff” (John R. Eardley to Williams, Hollister, California, [May] 1878, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to John R. Eardley, 1871–1880). Williams wrote of him as “Moss in Nevada” in August 1873 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1870–1873).

name: Moss, Mary
text: Probably Mary Brabin (1810–1883), wife of Joseph Moss, born at Leigh, Lancashire; she died at Austin, Nevada (FamilySearch KWJ4-JBY, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of her (9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 41659).

name: Moss, Edward
text: Probably Edward Moss (1835–1889), son of Joseph and Mary Moss, born at Ashton-under-Lyne (FamilySearch KWJW-H35, probable match). Held to bail after the siege as “Ed. Moss” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Family Tree records his enlistment at Camp Douglas, the post of Connor’s California Volunteers, in February 1863, and his discharge in 1866; he died at Austin, Nevada, in 1889. The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 41657).

name: Moss, James
text: Probably James Moss (1844–1915), son of Joseph and Mary Moss, born at Ashton-under-Lyne; in Nevada by 1870, he died at Boise, Idaho (FamilySearch KWVP-QWL, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 41655).

name: Chamberlain, James
text: Probably James Chamberlain (1848–1925), born at the Cape of Good Hope, son of Mary Allen Chamberlain, who is also on the roll with two of her daughters; he died at Salt Lake City (FamilySearch KWCY-SXF, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 37732).

name: Cowan, James Jr.
text: Probably James Cowan (1833–1895), born at Glasgow, son of James and Janet Cowan, who are also on the roll; he died at Slaterville (FamilySearch KWC4-JQV, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (3 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 42274). A James Cowan was called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67); which of the two James Cowans on the roll is not settled.

name: Park, Ann
text: Probably Ann Brooks Park (1811–1889), born at Cambuslang, Lanarkshire, wife of David Park; the family went to the Carson Valley, Nevada, where she died (FamilySearch KWJ5-6FF, probable match). She was not related to the Brooks family on the roll. The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of her (two files, 11 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 22908).

name: Moss, Peter
text: Peter I. Moss, named in the complaint after the November 1861 fight at the schoolhouse (Anderson, p. 82); a revelation of March 22, 1862, concerns his imprisonment (Spirit Prevails, pp. 471–72). Probably Peter John Moss (1837–1883), son of Joseph and Mary Moss, held to bail after the siege as “Peter J. Moss” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); he died in Idaho in 1883 (FamilySearch KWJC-HWG, probable match). Forscutt records his arrest at Farmington in March 1862: he was tried, fined and sentenced to forty days at hard labor, and wrote to his wife, “I shall not flinch from my principles” (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University; the entry is written “Mar 17/63,” but its place in the diary puts it in 1862).

name: Higham, Charles
text: Charles Higham (1823–1891), born in England, who came to Utah with his wife Jane in the Robert L. Campbell Company of 1854 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch LV14-G51). Held to bail after the siege as “Chas. Higham” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); Holley names him among the Slaterville and Marriott men taken prisoner (Holley, UHQ 2008). About 1877 George Williams wrote from England that “Bro Higham that was at Weber & now lives out Snake river” had visited George Thompson there and told “of great trouble with Indians” (Williams to William James, Church History Library, MS 31876). He died at Blackfoot, Idaho, in 1891. His wife Jane was George Thompson’s sister (see her note).

name: Higham, Jane
text: Jane Thompson (1824–1894), born in England, wife of Charles Higham, also on the roll; married in 1850, they crossed together in the Robert L. Campbell Company of 1854 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch K2VD-7R9). She died on June 5, 1894, in Bonneville County, Idaho, the day after she and her brother George were thrown against a bridge abutment by a runaway horse near what is now Ririe (FamilySearch K2VD-7R9; Anderson, Revisited , p. 211). She was the elder sister of George Thompson (1826–1894), Williams’s companion at Walthamstow and later president of the Montana church: both were christened at Ashwicken, Norfolk, children of Thomas Thompson and Jane Hunter (FamilySearch K2VD-7R9, K2JF-6VH). In 1891 Thompson, widowed, settled at Basalt, Idaho, near his daughter Emma, and wrote that “my sister Mrs. Higham” lived about four miles north (Thompson to Eardley, October 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1891). She is buried at Grove City Cemetery, Blackfoot.

name: Klingbeck, Jacob C.
text: Jacob Carl Frantsen Klingbech (1812–1897), born in Denmark, who came to Utah with his wife Karen Marie and their children in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859, the Danish company that also brought the Hanson, Christoffersen and Sorenson families on the roll (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch L4SL-HCW). In 1860 the family was at Moroni, Sanpete County, where he was enumerated as Jacob C. Clingbeck, farmer, with Caroline M. and Fredk W. (1860 U.S. census, Sanpete County). His brother Johan (roll: Solsan F.) baptized him into the Reorganized Church in the Payette Valley, Idaho, on May 23, 1872, and he was enrolled in the Mottsville branch in Nevada (Johan F. F. Klingbaek journal, circa 1857–1877, MS 8268, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). The Reorganized Church’s Danish Mission Fund lists a gift on December 17, 1874, from “J. C. Clengbak, Idaho” ( Saints’ Herald 22, 1875, p. 94). He died at Emmett, Idaho, in 1897.

name: Klingbeck, Karen M.
text: Karen Marie Christensen (1824–1898), born in Denmark, wife of Jacob Carl Klingbech since 1843 (FamilySearch L4SL-HXF); in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 with her husband and children (Church History Biographical Database). The 1860 census at Moroni gives her as Caroline M. (1860 U.S. census, Sanpete County).

name: Klingbeck, Frederick V.
text: Frederik Waerenth (Verner) Klingbech (1850–1931), born in Denmark, son of Jacob Carl and Karen Marie Klingbech, with whom he crossed in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch MNJV-Z9R). About eleven in 1861.

name: Nuttor, William
text: William Nutter (1830–1906), born in England, who came to Utah with his wife Dinah in the John Smith Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJW-4FB); the roll spells the name Nuttor. They later settled in Nebraska, where he died at Shelton, Buffalo County, in 1906.

name: Nuttor, Dinah
text: Dinah Ingham (1834–1918), born in England, wife of William Nutter since 1852; they crossed together in the John Smith Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJ4-VQY). She died at Shelton, Nebraska, in 1918.

name: White, William
text: William J. White (1841–1917), born in England, son of William and Rhoda White, who came to Utah with his mother (the roll’s Rhoda Jones) and his sisters Hannah and Sarah (the roll’s Sarah Harris) in the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch LCCL-MLL). Held to bail after the siege as “William White” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); Holley names him among the Slaterville and Marriott men taken prisoner (Holley, UHQ 2008). Family Tree gives his marriage in 1862 to Mary Cook, also on the roll; their children were born in the Carson Valley, Nevada, from 1863. He died at Spokane, Washington, in 1917. On November 9, 1875, John R. Eardley wrote from Hollister, California, that “Wm. White has also settled a few miles from here” (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 23); whether this was William J. White, whose family is placed in the Carson Valley, is not certain.

name: White, Hannah
text: Hannah White (1844–1868), born in England, daughter of William and Rhoda White and sister of William J. White and Sarah Harris, all on the roll with their mother as Rhoda Jones; she crossed with them in the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJW-43K). She married in 1864 and died at Dayton, Nevada, in the Carson Valley where many Morrisites settled, in 1868.

name: Mather, John O.
text: Called to the apostleship with Richard J. Livingstone, March 25, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 476), and held to bail after the siege as “J. O. Mather” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Probably John Ogilvie Mather (1822–1910), born in Scotland, who came to Utah in the Milo Andrus Company of 1855 with his wife Mary Magee and their children, among them Helen, born in 1851 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJD-2KP, probable match); the roll lists Mary and Ellen Mather with him. He died at Salt Lake City in 1910. A second Mather family, that of James Higginson Mather, came the same year in another company; the roll’s James Mather may belong to it.

name: Mather, Mary
text: Probably Mary Magee (1822–1888), born in Scotland, wife of John Ogilvie Mather since 1845, who crossed with him in the Milo Andrus Company of 1855 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch M1VV-GHK, probable match). Magee is also a surname on the roll; a family tie to William Magee has not been checked. She died at Salt Lake City in 1888.

name: Mather, Ellen
text: Probably Helen Mather (1851–1919), born at Dundee, daughter of John Ogilvie and Mary Mather, both on the roll; Helen and Ellen were used for the same name (FamilySearch KWJD-LSY, probable match). About ten in 1861. She died at Salt Lake City in 1919.

name: Astel, Joseph
text: Brought word to Morris that George Leslie wanted to hear from him; named in Morris’s letter to Leslie, Weber, July 9, 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 670). Summoned with the second group before the Farmington court-martial for refusing militia training, and fined $56.80 (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 34). Probably Joseph Astle (1829–1862), born in England, who came to Utah with his wife Esther in the Henry W. Miller Company of 1852 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch K27Y-ZFV, probable match). Family Tree gives his death in 1862, with the place as Montana; neither has been checked.

name: Astel, Esther
text: Probably Esther Bamford (1829–1887), born in England, wife of Joseph Astle since 1850, who crossed with him in the Henry W. Miller Company of 1852 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KDMD-WDN, probable match). She remarried in 1864 and died in Montana, where many Morrisites settled, in 1887.

name: Nash, George
text: Probably George Nash (born 1820 in England), who came to Utah with Maria Mitson in the Daniel Robison Company of 1860, the company that brought Mark Hill Forscutt (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJW-263, probable match). Nothing more about him is known yet.

name: Nash, Maria
text: Probably Maria Mitson (born 1817 in England), wife of George Nash in Family Tree, who crossed with him in the Daniel Robison Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KH9K-H9F, probable match).

name: Hegg, Svend
text: Probably Sven Olasson Hägg (1832–after 1882), a Swede who came to Utah in 1859, was held to bail after the siege; his wife Anna was very probably the second woman shot at the surrender on June 15, 1862 ( Deseret News , June 25, 1862; Spirit Prevails , p. 8; Gilbert, 1882, pp. 372–73). He wintered at Deer Lodge in 1865–66, joined William W. Davies’s association, and came with its first families to Walla Walla in 1867, where he was Davies’s spokesman until about 1877 and testified for him in 1881 (MS 31876, folder 22; Cilley et al. v. Davies , 1880–81). He proved up a homestead in Walla Walla County, patented in 1890 (BLM General Land Office records).

name: Babbington, Thomas
text: Probably Thomas Bebbington (1801–1866), born in England, who came to Utah in the Robert L. Campbell Company of 1854, the company of the Kendell and Higham families on the roll (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch LHDG-13K, probable match). He died at Ogden in 1866.

name: Baxter, Henry
text: Probably Henry Baxter (1806–1865), born in Scotland, who came to Utah with his family in the John A. Hunt Company of 1856 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJJ-G92, probable match). His wife Agnes Grant died in 1860, so the roll’s Agnes Baxter is perhaps another member of the family. A “Mrs. Baxter” was later in James Dove’s Morrisite group (Anderson, p. 178); which Baxter is not known. He died in Cache County in 1865.

name: Loasle, John C.
text: Hans Kasper (John Kasper) Loosli (1831–1901), born at Dürrenroth, Bern, Switzerland, who married Anna Elisabeth Hunsperger, the roll’s Anne Elizabeth Loasle, in 1857 and came to Utah in the James Darling Ross Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWNF-BGT). Held to bail after the siege as “J. G. Lousley” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Family Tree records later marriages in Utah from 1881, one of them in the Endowment House in 1882, which suggests he returned to the Latter-day Saints; he died at Clarkston, Cache County, in 1901.

name: Loasle, Anne Elizabeth
text: Anna Elisabeth Hunsperger (1835–1923), born in Switzerland, wife of Hans Kasper Loosli since 1857, with whom she came to Utah in the James Darling Ross Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWNF-BGR). She died in Utah in 1923..

name: Trahern, John
text: Probably John W. Treharne (born 1824), who crossed in the James Darling Ross Company of 1860, the company of the Bar and Rodgers families on the roll (Church History Biographical Database), and probably the “John Trehan” held to bail after the siege (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Not yet found in Family Tree.

name: Jones, William
text: Probably William Jones (born 1803 in England), who married Rhoda White, the roll’s Rhoda Jones, about 1860; Family Tree records him in Weber County in 1860 and his excommunication from the LDS Church at Weber on March 31, 1861 (FamilySearch LWFK-BKP, probable match). He is not the William J. Jones whose capture and detention at the fort in the spring of 1862 brought the posse (see Jones, William J.); which of the two the other references to a William Jones mean has not been settled. He is probably the “father Jones” of Slaterville who sheltered Morris in 1860 and told him, “You are a prophet of God” (George S. and James Dove, A Voice from the West , 1879, p. 6; The Spirit Prevails , p. 4).

name: Jones, Rhoda
text: Rhoda White (1811–1890), born at Bricketwood, Hertfordshire, widow of William White (died 1842), who came to Utah in the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 with her children William J., Hannah and Sarah White, all three on the roll, Sarah as Sarah Harris (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJQ-PBL). She married William Jones, who precedes her on the roll, about 1860. She went to Nevada with her children and died at Dayton, in the Carson Valley, in 1890. She is probably the “Mother Jones” of Slaterville who advised Morris how to avoid his enemies in 1860; the Doves call her “mother White, formerly mother Jones,” baptized into their San Francisco church on June 9, 1877, and record her testimony of what Morris said of the young George Dove ( A Voice from the West , 1879, pp. 6–7, 15, 26). The identification is probable, not proven.

name: Nielson, Christian
text: Remanded to prison with Peter Klemgaard after the siege, while the other men were held to bail (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to twelve years at hard labor, the second-heaviest sentence; the defence called Robert T. Burton to testify about him (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Pardoned a few days later by Governor Harding (Spirit Prevails, p. 8, and Gems, p. 31, as Christian Nelsen or Nelson).

name: Christiansen, Jens
text: At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to ten years at hard labor, and he was also named among the men tried for resisting an officer (Deseret News, April 1, 1863); pardoned a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31).

name: Mason, Andrew
text: Probably the Andrew M. Mason convicted of murder in the second degree at the March 1863 term and sentenced to ten years at hard labor (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The Spirit Prevails and Gems do not name him among the seven, listing John E. Jones in his place (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31).

name: Lee, George
text: The Spirit Prevails and Gems name a George Lee among the seven Morrisites sentenced in March 1863 (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31), but the court report names Andrew Lee, also on the roll, and no George Lee (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). A George Lee, 71, born in New York, was living at Walla Walla in June 1880, two houses from William W. Davies, among other former Morrisites (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c); whether he is the roll’s George Lee is not known. A George Lee testified against William W. Davies before the referee at Walla Walla in December 1880: he was “seventy years of age,” first met Davies at San Francisco “in ’70,” lived “in the camp fifteen months under Davies’ command,” gave Davies $1,200 to $1,300 in money and presents, and had believed “that the boy Jesus would control and rule the Kingdom of God on earth for his father”; his was the first of several claims brought to wind up the camp ( Walla Walla Statesman , January 1, 1881, p. 2; checked against the page image). He is surely the George Lee of the 1880 census; whether either is the roll’s George Lee is still not known.

name: Nielson, John
text: Held to bail after the siege as “John Neilson” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) and named among the men tried for resisting an officer in March 1863 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The Spirit Prevails and Gems name a John Nielson among the seven sentenced for murder (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31); the court report has a “Kadrup Neilsen” among the seven instead.

name: Hewitt, Philip
text: Testified for the defence at the trial of Peter Klemgard and others, March 1863 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Perhaps Phillip Hewitt (1803–1882), who came to Utah in 1855 (Church History Biographical Database); not yet confirmed. A Philip Hewitt testified at Burton’s trial in February 1879 that he lived in Salt Lake City’s Twelfth Ward, had been at the camp in 1862 and was a Morrisite ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 25, 1879).

name: Svenson, Peter
text: Testified for the defence at the trial of Peter Klemgard and others, March 1863 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Perhaps the Peter Swenson (born 1836) of the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database); not yet confirmed.

name: Rasmussen, Hans C.
text: Hans Christian Rasmussen (born 1816 in Denmark; FamilySearch L6NP-CJX), husband of Caroline Henriette Holm (the roll’s Caroline H.) and father of Peter Frederik Christian and Georg Thorvald (the roll’s Peter F.C. and George T.). The 1870 U.S. census finds the family at Walla Walla, Washington Territory, as “H C Rassmussen”, 54, with children born in Denmark, Utah (about 1860), Idaho (about 1863) and Montana (about 1866), a path that follows the Morrisite settlements at Soda Springs and Deer Lodge.

name: Rasmussen, Caroline H.
text: Caroline Henriette Holm (born 1824 in Denmark; FamilySearch MVC9-941), wife of Hans Christian Rasmussen. Family Tree records her emigration in 1860. She is the “Lena”, 46, of the 1870 U.S. census at Walla Walla.

name: Rasmussen, Peter F.C.
text: Peter Frederik Christian Rasmussen (born 1846 in Denmark; FamilySearch G4PW-RR7), son of Hans Christian and Caroline Henriette Rasmussen; his given names match the roll’s initials. Nothing later is recorded for him in Family Tree.

name: Rasmussen, George T.
text: Georg Thorvald Rasmussen (1848–1916; born at Copenhagen; FamilySearch G4PW-GL6), son of Hans Christian and Caroline Henriette Rasmussen; “Thorvald” matches the roll’s T. With his parents at Walla Walla in the 1870 U.S. census, age 21; he married Elmira Adalaid Cox in 1874 and died in Washington County, Oregon.

name: Livingstone, R. J.
text: Richard John Livingston (1828–1892), born at Liverpool, was called to the Morrisite apostleship in March 1862, held to bail after the siege, and fined $100 for resisting an officer in 1863 ( Spirit Prevails , p. 476; Deseret News , April 1, 1863). He farmed in Carson Valley, Nevada, from the 1860s and was a leader among the scattered Morrisites there, then moved in 1877 to Walla Walla to join William W. Davies, whom he soon turned against ( Carson Valley News , 1876–78; Eardley to Williams, 1878, MS 31876). He died at Walla Walla in 1892 ( Saints’ Herald 39, 1892, p. 438). In April 1877 the Reorganized Church’s paper reported that “Elder Livingstone of the Walla Walla church had been preaching there at Genoa” ( Saints’ Herald 24, April 1, 1877, p. 105).

name: Livingstone, Isabella
text: Isabella Napier (1818–1895; FamilySearch L41L-NPL), wife of Richard John Livingston from 1860, after an earlier marriage in 1850. In 1880 she and her husband were living at Walla Walla (1880 U.S. census). She died in Washington in 1895. The “Mrs. Levengston” who put $900 into William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla and later got it back, according to testimony in 1881, was probably Isabella (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Hanson, Lars Christian
text: Lars Christian Hansen (1832–1889; born at Dronninglund, Denmark; FamilySearch KC44-FBW), husband of Mattie Maria Iverson (the roll’s Mattie Hanson). The land office’s ledger of claims, its tract book, gives two dates for his claim to 160 acres west of Deer Lodge: March 2, 1865, probably when he settled on the land, and April 26, 1869, when he filed, the same day as his neighbour Niels R. Beck. He paid for the land in June 1872 with land scrip, a federal certificate that could be used instead of money; an Ellen C. Jensen used the next certificate the same day for land nearby (Bureau of Land Management tract book, Montana, vol. 5, p. 96, township 8 north, range 9 west; images on FamilySearch, “United States, Bureau of Land Management Tract Books”). The 1870 U.S. census finds him farming in the Deer Lodge Valley as “Lewis C. Hansen”, 38, with Mary 38, Joseph 8 (born in Utah) and two children born in Montana. He died at Deer Lodge in 1889. He received two land titles (patents): one in 1873 for the land paid with scrip, next to Niels R. Beck’s, and one for 634.84 acres, nearly a square mile, bought for cash and patented on March 5, 1890, after his death (BLM General Land Office records, accessions AGS-0353-237 and STA-MT0140__.418). Why one farmer bought so much land is an open question.

name: Hanson, Mattie
text: Mattie Maria Iverson (1830–1897; FamilySearch LYV6-TPP), wife of Lars Christian Hansen; the “Mary” of the 1870 U.S. census at Deer Lodge. She died in Montana in 1897.

name: Olsen, Ole
text: ## Denmark and Kington Fort, 1810–62 Probably Ole Olsen (1810–1888; FamilySearch KHLF-L26), who died at Deer Lodge. He was among the men discharged at the fort on June 16, 1862, aged 54 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). His daughter Karen Marie (born 1843) was probably the Danish wife of Joseph Morris; see the notes for Karen Morris and Anne Olsen, which also give the family’s 1855, 1859 and 1860 records. ## Deer Lodge, 1870–88 The 1870 U.S. census lists Ole Olsen, 60, born in Denmark, farming in the Deer Lodge Valley ($300 real estate, $700 personal), with Josephine 8, born in Utah; Family Tree gives him a daughter Josephine Victoria, born 1861. Family Tree also gives him a son Lars Olsen (1837–1908); whether he is the roll’s Lars Olsen is not confirmed. On June 30, 1876, Ole Olsen received a patent for 160 acres in the Deer Lodge Valley, paid for with Virginia agricultural college scrip (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, secs. 26–27; BLM General Land Office records, accession AGS-0353-411). A Lars Olsen’s scrip patent, signed the same day, covers adjoining land in section 27. The Montana church’s membership record supports the identification: Josephine Victoria Olsen, born at South Weber, Utah, on December 22, 1861, was baptized at Deer Lodge on June 17, 1876, by Jens Jensen and George Johnson and confirmed by Jens Jensen and Ole Olsen (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1

name: Gudmundson, Christian
text: Christian Nielsen Garff (1848–1927; born at Eskebjerg, Denmark; FamilySearch KWDS-VMD), son of Marie Jacobsdatter (the roll’s Mary Gudmundson) by her first marriage, and so stepson of Gudmund Gudmundson. The 1870 U.S. census lists him as Christian, 22, born in Denmark, in Goodman Goodmanson’s household in Salt Lake County. He died at Logan in 1927.

name: Richardson, Jane
text: Probably Jean or Jane Miller (born 1815 in Scotland; FamilySearch GNP1-NDS), wife of James Richardson (born 1810 at Edinburgh; GMQL-V7P), the first James Richardson on the roll; the second is probably their son James (born 1834; GNP1-ZYN). Family Tree places the family at Alton, Illinois, in 1850 and in Douglas County, Nebraska, in 1860. The 1870 U.S. census finds them in the Deer Lodge Valley: James 62, blacksmith; Jane 59; James 36 and William 32, farmers; Alexander 24 and Cornelius 17, miners, born in Illinois. Alexander may be the roll’s “Aerilous”: the bail list prints “Alexander Richardson” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) and the court report “Alex. Richardson” (Deseret News, April 1, 1863).

name: Richardson, William
text: Probably William Richardson (born 1838 in Scotland; FamilySearch GNP1-C87), son of James and Jane Richardson; farming in his father’s household in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870 U.S. census, age 32. Family Tree has a possible duplicate, PN4F-6R3 (1839–1913), who died at Boise. A William Richardson received a patent for land in the Deer Lodge Valley paid with agricultural college scrip, signed June 30, 1876 (Montana Principal Meridian, T7N R9W, sec. 21; BLM General Land Office records, accession AGS-0353-406), and a James Richardson, the father or the son of that name, another nearby in 1880 (sec. 16; accession AGS-0435-027).

name: Bright, Benjamin
text: Benjamin Bright (1850–1927; born in Pottawattamie County, Iowa; FamilySearch KGKV-MXW), son of John G. Bright and Ann Cook, the roll’s John and Ann Bright. The 1860 U.S. census lists him at 9, born in Iowa, and the 1870 U.S. census at 19, a farm hand, both times in his parents’ household (in 1870 under the Kaysville post office, Davis County). He married Josephine Wright Earl in 1890 and died at South Weber in 1927. (Corrected November 4, 2026: an earlier link pointed to a Benjamin Bright born in England in 1855, who reached Utah only in 1867.)

name: Olsen, Lars
text: Perhaps Lars Olsen (1837–1908), whom Family Tree gives as a son of Ole Olsen (Olsen, Ole); not yet confirmed. A Lars Olsen received two patents for land in the Deer Lodge Valley next to Ole Olsen’s: one paid with agricultural college scrip, signed June 30, 1876, the same day as Ole’s (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, sec. 27), and a 160-acre cash entry patented in 1884 (sec. 22) (BLM General Land Office records, accessions AGS-0353-427 and STA-MT0090__.275). The 1880 U.S. census lists “Lars Oleson”, born in Denmark about 1838, as head of a household at Cottonwood Creek in the Deer Lodge Valley, where Niels R. Beck and Lars C. Hansen also lived (1880 U.S. census); the age fits Ole Olsen’s son.

name: Hanson, Andrus
text: Probably Andrew Hansen (1844–1926), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, who died at Deer Lodge, Montana (FamilySearch 2Z8Q-CHW); the roll also has an Andrus Hanson Jr., so which entry is his is not certain. An Anders Hansen received a patent for a 160-acre cash entry in the Deer Lodge Valley on June 20, 1883 (Montana Principal Meridian, T9N R9W, sec. 33; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0090__.152). In September 1925 a visitor from the RLDS reunion in Montana called on “Andrew Hanson,” “a little Dane, eighty-one years old,” and his sister Mrs. Bernard, 71, after photographing the Lord’s House ( Saints’ Herald 72, September 23, 1925, p. 1012).

name: Hanson, Niels
text: Niels Hansen (1851–1938), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson; at Deer Lodge, Montana, by 1870, and died there (FamilySearch KFK2-MSL). A Niels Hansen, probably he, received a patent for the northeast quarter of section 32 (Montana Principal Meridian, T9N R9W) in the Deer Lodge Valley on February 29, 1896, next to Anders Hansen’s land in section 33 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0260__.484).

name: Garrett, John
text: Probably John Garrett (1815–1899), born in England, who died at Blackfoot, Idaho (FamilySearch K2W8-44D, probable match). The 1870 U.S. census lists Jno. Garrett, 50, born in England, a fur trader, with Martha, 50, at a mining camp in Oneida County, Idaho; the roll and Family Tree name his wife Thurza. The 1880 U.S. census settles it: John Garrett, 65, and his wife Thirza, 75, both born in England, were living at Blackfoot, Oneida County, Idaho (1880 U.S. census, Blackfoot, ED 27, p. 323b), so the 1870 “Martha” was probably an enumerator’s error. Between 1882 and 1892 a John Garrett received four patents for land near Blackfoot (Boise Meridian, T3S R35E), each under a different law: a 158.45-acre cash entry (1882), a 160-acre homestead (1888), 200 acres under the Desert Land Act (1890) and a Timber Culture Act claim (1892) (BLM General Land Office records, accessions STA-ID0010__.017, STA-ID0110__.415, STA-ID0020__.148 and TC-0144-330).

name: Park, David Sr.
text: David Park (1809–1884), born at Cambuslang, Lanarkshire, Scotland, husband of Ann Brooks, also on the roll (FamilySearch LLQF-CF6). He received one of the earliest land patents in Carson Valley, Nevada, where many Morrisites settled: a 160-acre cash entry at the Carson City land office, patented December 10, 1864 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, secs. 1–2; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0010__.049). Family Tree places him in Douglas County, Nevada, in 1870. In June 1880 he was at Walla Walla among the members of William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven: “David Park”, 71, born in Scotland, a laborer, sharing a dwelling with Ole Hagg two houses from Davies (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c). He returned to the Carson Valley and died at Mottsville on July 22, 1884 (FamilySearch). A list of donations filed in the 1880 suit against Davies credits David Park with $320 between 1874 and 1878 (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Bull, William F.
text: A William F. Bull received a patent for 160 acres near Genoa in Carson Valley, Nevada, where many Morrisites settled, on May 10, 1866 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, sec. 9; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0010__.258). He is very probably the roll’s William F. Bull: William Field Bull (1819–1896), husband of Agnes Cowan, also on the roll, died at Mottsville in the Carson Valley (FamilySearch KWJN-719), and the 1880 U.S. census lists “W. F. Bull”, born in England about 1820, in the Carson Valley, Douglas County, with his wife Agnes and children born in Utah (James C., about 1860) and Nevada (1872–1879) (1880 U.S. census).

name: Sorenson, Brooer
text: Probably Bror Sörensson (1807–1902), born in Sweden, who died at Walla Walla, Washington (FamilySearch L56J-MC2, probable match); Family Tree gives him two marriages, the second in 1861, and his daughter Celia is also on the roll. In June 1880 a “Sorenson”, 73, born in Sweden, a laborer, was living at Walla Walla among the members of William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven, with a wife of 45 and children Annie, 18, August, 16, and Isaac, 13, born in Utah, and Lena E., 10, born in Washington Territory (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 264, dwelling 12). The same suit’s list of donations credits “Brrer Sorensen” with a yoke of cattle in 1867, and a witness recalled that “one Mrs. Sorensen” left the community with cattle and a wagon. Testifying for Davies in 1881, Broer Sorenson, 72, said he had known Davies since 1861 and had come with him from Montana in 1867 with his wife and five children, when the community was only five families; he then lived two and a half miles from the camp. Davies named the Sorenson family among those who came with him (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Williams, Thomas
text: A Thomas Williams testified at Robert T. Burton’s trial in February 1879 that he had lived in Ogden since 1865 and had been at South Weber, “called Morris camp,” part of the time in 1862, and was there when the camp was attacked ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 22, 1879). The name is common, and whether he is the Thomas Williams of the roll is not confirmed.

name: Thompson, Emma
text: ## Kington Fort and Soda Springs, 1850–64 Daughter of George Thompson, later president of the Montana church, and his wife Frances; born in 1850, the only one of their six children to survive (Anderson, p. 210). As Emma Thompson Just she wrote to a cousin in England in 1864 describing the journey to Soda Springs in May 1863 and the first year there (quoted in Anderson, p. 161). ## Burton’s trial, 1879 At Burton’s trial in February 1879 “Mrs. Emma Just” testified for the prosecution that she lived in the Snake River valley, Oneida County, Idaho, and had been with the Morrisites on the Weber in 1862 ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 22, 1879). The fuller report has her describe the cellar where her family and her aunt’s sheltered, the shooting of Mrs. Bowman, and her father sitting on Morris’s body; she said the man on the dark horse shot Morris and Mrs. Bowman, which the defence used against her, since Stoddard rode the black horse ( Salt Lake Weekly Tribune , March 1, 1879, p. 5; Deseret Evening News , March 5, 1879, p. 3). ## Idaho By the account her daughter Agnes Just Reid published in 1923 as letters from Emma to her father in London, Emma had been divorced in about 1868, left Montana for an aunt’s home in Idaho, and married Nels Just before a justice of the peace at Malad in November 1870; they settled on the Blackfoot River, and her neighbors there included the Garretts of the roll (see John Garrett). Williams wrote from Walthamstow in February 1875 that “Bro Just has a son who

name: Thomas, William W.
text: Probably William Watkin Thomas of Gwendale, in the upper Deer Lodge valley, Montana. W. P. Thomas named “W. W. Thomas” among the Welsh men at Kington Fort on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862 (W. P. Thomas, letter of May 30, 1862, MS 31876, folder 21; translation generated by Claude). No source yet ties him by name to the 1861–62 roll. This fits Black’s W. W. Thomas, a Welshman baptized into the RLDS Church in 1865 who died in the upper Deer Lodge Valley in 1879. His Herald obituary gives his death there on September 29, 1879, “of congestion of the brain,” aged 50, born in Wales, emigrated to Utah in 1853, baptized into the Reorganized Church at Malad City in 1865; an earlier notice, very probably of the same man, has “William H. Thomas,” who joined at Malad in 1865, dying at Deer Lodge on September 5, 1879 ( Saints’ Herald 28, September 1, 1881, p. 307; 26, November 1, 1879, p. 336). His wife was Margaret. A William Watkins Thomas took S½ NW¼ and N½ SW¼ sec. 4, T4N R10W, just north of the Evans and Jessen homesteads, with agricultural college scrip, patented June 1, 1872 (BLM General Land Office records, accession AGS-0353-021). The New North-West names a W. Watkins Thomas, “who has had extensive experience in that business in Wales,” building the roasters and dryers for a works there in 1875; a W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee of the Gwendale railroad meeting of April 1875; a W W Thomas of Gwendale in 1877; and William Watkin Thomas as an administrator of a neigh

name: Thomas, W. P.
text: Probably William Price Thomas (born 1813, Carmarthenshire), a Welsh Latter-day Saint baptized a Morrisite at South Weber, who marched with the infantry on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862 (letter to his family, MS 31876, folder 21). By the mid-1860s he had settled on Warm Springs Creek in the Deer Lodge Valley, where the Montana church was organized at his house in 1872 with him as first counselor to William James (Morris, Anaconda, Montana , p. 15; MS 32226).
