He went on a mission to Wales in 1869, quarreled with Daniel James and drifted from Williams in the 1870s, and patented his homestead near the future Anaconda in 1880 (MS 31876; BLM General Land Office records).

name: Morris, Karen
text: Probably Karen Marie Olsen, born at Melby, Frederiksborg, Denmark, on March 28, 1843, daughter of Ole Olsen and Ane Jensdatter (Melby parish register, births, 1843, no. 4; FamilySearch KHXH-CV5), and, if so, the Danish wife of Joseph Morris whom the movement’s history calls “Mary Olsen,” married in August 1861 ( The Spirit Prevails , “History of Events,” p. 5); “Mary” would be her middle name, Marie, so the roll’s Mary Morris may be the same woman entered twice. She came from Zealand with her parents and siblings on the William Tapscott in 1859, aged 16 (Saints by Sea, BMR p. 116), in the Robert F. Neslen Company (Church History Biographical Database), and is “Caroline,” 17, in Ole Olsen’s household in Salt Lake County in July 1860 (1860 U.S. census, Salt Lake County, Utah, p. 219). The movement’s own account fits her family: after the surrender Morris’s widow took possession of the chest of revelations, and “her father, after her death, sold it to Abraham Taylor,” who kept it more than twenty years before 1886 ( The Spirit Prevails , “Concerning the Revelations,” p. 3). So the widow died by the mid-1860s and her father outlived her and stayed among the Morrisites, as Ole Olsen did (he died at Deer Lodge in 1888); in 1878 James Bowman also mentions a debt of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). No record yet names her as Morris’s wife, and none found gives her death. See the notes for Mary Morris and for

name: Morris, Mary
text: ## Morris’s wife of 1861 Probably Mary Olsen, a Danish convert and the wife of Joseph Morris; the movement’s own history says he married “Mary Olsen, a Dane,” in August 1861 (Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” p. 5). After a revelation of August 23, 1861, told Morris to look for “a faithful companion,” he married her shortly afterward; a revelation less than a month after the wedding addressed discord between them, and she remained with him (Anderson, p. 87; Spirit Prevails, pp. 149–51). Their infant son died soon after birth in May 1862 (Anderson, pp. 104–5). ## His earlier marriages Morris’s earlier marriages had all ended before South Weber. He married Mary Thorp at Mottram in Longdendale, Cheshire, in February 1847; in April 1854 he petitioned the Sanpete probate court for a divorce, and in July she married Henry Beal at Ephraim, where she died in 1905 (see the Chronology, March–April 1854). The widow Elizabeth Mills, whom he married in 1855, left him in about six months; at Provo in 1857 he married Elizabeth Jones, from whom, George writes, “those in Athoraty” separated him (Anderson, pp. 35, 41; George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, pp. 115, 117–19). In 1876 George had “Joseph Morris Jr and Mary his wife” sealed by proxy without saying which Mary (George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, pp. 115, 117–19, 187). ## Karen Marie Olsen Anderson does not mention the roll’s Karen Morris. Morris’s Danish wife was probably Karen Marie Olsen, born at Melby, Frederiksborg, Denmark

name: Olsen, Anne
text: ## The family in Denmark and Utah Probably the wife of Ole Olsen (Olsen, Ole), whose name follows hers on the roll, with Lars Olsen after him. Family Tree gives Ole Olsen a wife Ane Jensdatter, born March 29, 1817, at Adserboe, Melby, Frederiksborg, Denmark, the mother of his children, among them Lars (1837–1908) and Josephine Victoria (1861–1907) (FamilySearch KHWN-B4R). The Danish census of 1855 lists the household at Melby: Ole Olsen 47, Ane Jensdatter 38, Lars 19, Maren Kirstine 17, Karen Marie 12, Peder Jensen 3, and a widow, Maren Jensen, born Jensdatter, 78. The family (Ole 49, Anna 42, Lars 21, Maren Kristina 21, Karen Marie 16, Peter Jensen 7 and the infant Juliane Johanna) sailed from Liverpool on the William Tapscott on April 11, 1859 (Saints by Sea, BMR p. 116), and in July 1860 Ole, Anna, Lars, “Caroline” (Karen Marie), Peter, Hannah and Maren, 80, were in one household in Salt Lake County (1860 U.S. census, Salt Lake County, Utah, p. 219). Family Tree also lists, without sources, the family’s emigration in 1859 on the William Tapscott and a residence in Salt Lake County in 1860. ## Death at Kington Fort, 1862 Family Tree gives her death only as before 1870, in the United States, with no source. A sketch of Josephine’s husband, George Johnson, written about 1902, says her mother Anna died in Wyoming in 1862 ( Progressive Men of the State of Montana , Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902], pp. 1092–93). C. LeRoy Anderson writes that Josephine, who married George Johnson

name: Lorensen, John Peter
text: Probably Johan Peter Lorentzen, born May 23, 1817, in Holmens parish, Copenhagen (FamilySearch KLVC-XHL), father of the roll’s Charles and Josephine E. Lorentzen. Family Tree does not give a date of death; it says only that he died before 1870, probably in Nevada. Before November 10, 2026, this guide gave his death as 1870 in Nevada, reading that estimate as a date. In the 1870 census his children Charles and Josephine were living at Treasure City, White Pine County, Nevada, in the household of Caroline Laurenson, 52, born in Denmark, with no husband listed (1870 U.S. census, White Pine Co., NV, dwelling 658).

name: Anderson, Christian
text: Probably the Christen Anderson whom the Montana church’s membership record, begun in July 1874, lists as born on Fyn, Denmark, on August 1, 1809, baptized at South Weber, Utah, on July 18, 1861, by Jens Mikkelson, and confirmed by J[oseph] Morris (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library, folder 7, p. 4). The name is common, and the match rests on the South Weber baptism in 1861, the year the roll was begun.

name: Rasmusson, Rasmus
text: ## Denmark and Weber, 1830–61 Probably the Rasmus Rasmussen whom the Montana church’s membership record, begun in July 1874, lists as born at Skallerup, Denmark, on October 28, 1830, and baptized at South Weber, Utah, on June 27, 1861; he baptized several of the Omaha and Council Bluffs converts in 1869 and 1870 (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library, folder 7, pp. 2–5). ## Omaha and Council Bluffs, 1869–76 On February 7, 1869, at Council Bluffs, he was made the church’s first bishop and “first President of the Aaronic order,” an office Williams had given him “according to his birthright” (Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876); in 1869 he was at Omaha City, and Williams called him “the presiding Bishop” there, to whom the accounts of a free-will offering fund were to be rendered (Williams to the Saints at Omaha and Council Bluffs, 1869, MS 31876). The Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists him first, as “President for Aaronic Præstedømme” [president of the Aaronic priesthood], born at “Akkerup,” Fyn, on October 28, 1830, and baptized at South Weber on June 27, 1861, and confirmed by Joseph Morris; the birthplace differs from the Montana record’s “Skallerup,” on the same date (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In July 18

name: James, William
text: ## Wales and Kington Fort Probably William M. James (William Morgan James, 1817–1903, in the Church History Library’s catalog), born in Wales and baptized at South Weber, Utah, the first name in the Montana church’s membership record begun in July 1874. He “surrendered during the engagement” of June 13–15, 1862, and was discharged at the fort on June 16 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; identification with the later Montana leader probable, not checked). ## Nevada and Montana, 1872–90 Appointed president at the organizing meeting of September 22, 1872, by Williams’s epistle of August; a revelation of August 22, 1872, had already called him “on a Mission to Nevada,” and he left “with a Teamster down to Corrine” (minutebook, September 1872–January 1874, MS 32226, Church History Library). In 1873 he was away on “his Mission in Nevada,” and he took back the presidency in Montana on July 20 that year. He presided over the Warm Spring Creek stake and the Montana council; in 1890 he said Williams and John R. Eardley had sent him from Nevada to preside over the Saints in Montana. On February 24, 1878, he presided at the joint council at Race Track that chose Andrew Hendrikson’s land for the Lord’s House, though he had favoured Warm Spring (council minutes, 1873–74 and 1878, MS 31876). Sustained as president of the church in Montana on April 25, 1883, by 19 votes to 10, he claimed the office for li

name: Merrick, John
text: A “John A. Merrick” was among the twenty absent when the names of those bound over were called at the March 1863 term, and his recognizance was declared forfeited ( Deseret News , March 18, 1863, p. 8). On September 13, 1871, George Williams wrote from England that “Bro Merrick” had set out for Montana “with his cattle,” and that Merrick had “passed thro the order of Birthright and at that time was set apart to preach in his native State”; in 1872 Williams said he had asked Merrick to aid “the European mission,” without reply (Williams to Andrew Hendrikson, MS 31876). Before he set out, on August 2, 1871, Williams had warned that the road ran through “a country of Indians” and counseled a good guard (translation from the Danish generated by Claude), and wrote that “he is accepted in the position he left me at Cottonwood”; in November 1871 he had no news yet of “Bro Merrick and Knudson” on the way (Williams to Hendrikson, August 2 and November 1871, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1871 and 1872–1873). Williams wrote in 1872 that Merrick's plan to visit Montana in March was “extraordinary for impudence,” though “when this man visited me at Cottonwood he had not shown a disposition so infamous” (Williams to Hendrikson, January 1872, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1872–1873). Possibly the John Merrick whom John R. Eardley, writing from Hollister, California, on November 9, 1875, described as li

name: Bryne, Moses
text: Moses Byrne (1820–1904), born in Cheshire, came to Utah in 1854 and settled at Slaterville; he married Catherine Cardon and Anne Beus, both on the roll (FamilySearch KWNJ-JZ2). He was one of the six men Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, to found his church, a week after the Slaterville Branch excommunicated him, but he was soon “cast off” (Price journal, P26-22 f1; Holley, UHQ 76, 2008, pp. 253–54; Young, Contributor 11, 1890, p. 281). By 1869 he ran the railroad station in western Wyoming that grew into Piedmont, where he died in 1904.

name: Price, Josiah
text: Josiah D. Price, born April 8, 1832, in Glamorgan, South Wales, by his own record. He was baptized on December 3, 1861, by William Davies and Edward Lloyd, confirmed by Richard Cook and ordained by Morris, and counted himself the “431st person” in the church; he recorded the consecration of property on December 30, 1861, and the oath of February 12, 1862, sworn twelve at a time, and translated Morris’s ordinances and oath into Welsh. His pocket journal, in English and Welsh, copies Morris’s ordinances and the inscription of his scepter, names the six whom Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, and describes the drill and the four horsemen of May 1, 1862, the companies and soldier’s oath of May 26, which he swore, and the Foreshadowing procession of May 30; it also holds a drawing of Morris’s worlds. On September 30, 1862, he sold a yoke of cattle to John E. Jones and hired himself to Jones from October 6 at fifty dollars a month. Bound over after the siege, he was absent when the names were called at the March 1863 term, and his recognizance was declared forfeited ( Deseret News , March 18, 1863, p. 8). Called for trial at the March 1863 term as “Josiah D. Price” (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). He was baptized into the Reorganized Church on February 3, 1867, by Robert Murdock, in Oneida County, Idaho Territory (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Lundgreen, Christian
text: Probably the Christian Lundgren whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born in Sjælland, Denmark, baptized at South Weber on June 30, 1861, and confirmed by Joseph Morris; an Aaronic priest, he was excluded from the Omaha congregation in 1870 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). On April 28, 1862, Mark H. Forscutt recorded at Kington Fort: “Christian Lundgreen whipped in the fort by 7 women. He had turned traitor, and also helped Mortensen’s wife away in the night time.” He names the women as Maryann Taylor, Amelia Rothwell, Isabella Bowman, Mrs. Sorenson and Mrs. Thomas (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). Forscutt’s Sketch tells the story without naming him.

name: Petersen, Hans
text: Probably the Hans Petersen whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born in Sjælland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber; his name is struck through, and he was excluded in 1870 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Peterson, Kershon
text: Probably Kjersten Petersen, whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born at Evetofte [?], Sjælland, Denmark, on December 6, 1821, and baptized at South Weber; she was a member of the Omaha congregation from 1869 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Larsen, Niel
text: Probably the Niels Larsen, born in Sjælland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Maren Larsen (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Larsen, Maren
text: Probably the Maren Larsen, born in Sjælland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Niels Larsen (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Christiansen, Mikkel C.
text: Probably the Mikkel Christensen, born in Jutland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Elisa Christensen; both names are struck through, and both were excluded on November 20, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Christiansen, Lese
text: Possibly the Elisa Christensen, born in Jutland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Mikkel Christensen; she was excluded on November 20, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). The identification rests on the names alone.

name: Guhl, Maren
text: Very probably Maren Sorensen (1802–1881), mother of S. P. Guhl and widow of Fredrick Christopher Guhl (1793–1841) (FamilySearch KWJJ-JWX, KFKG-KMG). The Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists a “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” born at Horsens, Jutland, and baptized at South Weber; by 1869 she was the wife of Carleton Fellows, and both were excluded on February 5, 1871 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Her husband Carleton Fellows was born at Buffalo, New York, and in November 1876 her son wrote from Council Bluffs that he had baptized his stepfather, “old Dr. Charleston Fallows,” into the Reorganized Church, and then “my mother” ( Saints’ Herald 23, December 15, 1876, p. 758). The roll’s Marian Guhl may then be his sister, Mary Louise Guhl (1823–1905, FamilySearch KC4Q-C9N), or his wife.

name: Guhl, Marian
text: The Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists a “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” born at Horsens, Jutland, and baptized at South Weber; that is very probably the roll’s Maren Guhl, S. P. Guhl’s mother (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Marian may be S. P. Guhl’s sister, Mary Louise Guhl (1823–1905, FamilySearch KC4Q-C9N), or his wife.

name: Bowen, John
text: Possibly the John D. Bowen of Austin, Lander County, Nevada, to whom a revelation of August 20, 1872, sent William James “to assist him in wisely arrangement in his affairs,” calling him “my son J. D. Bowen,” who “has been worthy and felt after my work.” The identification with the roll’s John Bowen is not checked. In September 1871 Williams wrote that he was glad Bowen meant to visit Montana; he “may have listened to Josephism,” but should be invited to settle at Deer Lodge “and to compose some suitable Hymns,” and thanked for “sending to my Family” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1870–1873). Bowen wrote in Welsh to William P. Thomas from Austin in 1872–74; in October 1874 he wrote that he had lost all his property, but that Cainan was a true prophet who had sent his servant two years before to try to save it (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to William P. and Margaret Thomas, 1871–1874; translation from the Welsh generated by Claude). In 1874, having lost his station between Ely and Eureka, he still wrote to W. P. Thomas from Austin that “it is impossible for Joseph Morris to be in error, nor Cainan his successor,” and that he read Cainan’s letters, copied into his book, to his wife (Bowen to Thomas, August 31, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to William P. and Margaret Thomas, 1871–1874; translation from the Welsh generated by Claude). In 1878, John R. Eardley reported, John Bowen was “e

name: Warner, Joseph
text: Joseph Warner (about 1816–1893), born in Hanover, came to Utah in 1856, was cut off from the LDS Church at Providence after a vision of Joseph Smith, joined Morris at Weber in May 1861, and was discharged at the fort after the siege ( Ogden Junction , February 22, 1879, p. 4; CR 100 397). About 1875 he travelled among the scattered Morrisites prophesying Joseph Morris’s return to Weber in 1876 (Eardley to William James, November 9, 1875, MS 31876). He testified at Robert T. Burton’s trial in 1879 and died, indigent, at South Weber in 1893 (Davis County Court minutes, October 1893).

name: Werner, Ingray
text: Possibly Ingry (Ingrid) Warner, wife of Joseph Warner, whom Family Tree gives as born in Sweden in 1811 and as dying on June 13, 1862, the day the posse’s first cannon shot killed two women at Kington Fort; the death date has no source there and has not been checked (FamilySearch Family Tree, GK43-KYD). See the open question “Who died at Kington Fort?”

name: Thompson, George
text: ## Kington Fort and Soda Springs, 1826–65 Probably George Thompson (1826–1894), later president of the Montana church, who gave his birth date as April 16, 1826, in a letter of 1880 (FamilySearch K2JF-6VH, probable match). At the surrender he sat down on Morris’s body and asked to be killed, saying he had “nothing now to live for,” until a man snapped a gun at him and he was dragged away, as his daughter Emma testified at Burton’s trial in 1879 ( Salt Lake Weekly Tribune , March 1, 1879, p. 5). He had lived in Idaho, and went from Soda Springs to Salt Lake City in 1865 to visit the Prophet Cainan (Anderson, p. 168). ## England, 1869–91 In 1869 he was a shoemaker at Ashwicken, near King’s Lynn, Norfolk, where Williams was preaching, and that December at Brighton; from June 1874 he kept a shop in Shernhall Street, Walthamstow, Essex, where Williams lived with him from January 1875 and where he did Williams’s writing in his last illness. In 1880 he planned to sell his business to take Williams to America. By August 1883 he had moved to Thornwood Common, near Epping, and wrote that “I say but little about gospels now … No one here believes as I do so I am very quiet” (Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1883, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874). He was elected president of the church in 1886. In his daughter Emma’s letters as published in 1923, he writes in 1891 that his business is sold and he is coming to her in Idaho

name: Lloyd, Edward
text: With William Davies he baptized Josiah D. Price on December 3, 1861 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Sorenson, Anders
text: Probably Anders Søndermark (Anders Sørensen in the draft), whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born at Vrensted, Jutland, Denmark, on January 9, 1821, and baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, by Morris and Mikkelsen; an Aaronic priest, he was excluded with his wife Karen Maria on November 30, 1871 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Sorenson, Kar M.
text: Probably Karen Maria Sørensen Søndermark, whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born at Vrensted, Jutland, Denmark, on October 9, 1822, and baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, with her husband Anders; both were excluded on November 30, 1871 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Kundson, Hans
text: Probably the Hans Knudsen whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists as born on Fyn, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber on July 18, 1861, by Jens Mikkelsen; at Omaha in 1869 he baptized converts with Rasmus Rasmussen and S. P. Guhl (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Richards, William
text: Probably the Welsh member at Box Elder whom masked men took from a neighbor’s house one night in the winter of 1861–62; he was spared on his oath never to return to Box Elder. Hearing that he had been killed, W. P. and W. W. Thomas fled to the camp at Weber, where Forscutt wrote down their account (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University).

name: Mather, James
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Anderson, p. 67). In August 1873 Mark H. Forscutt called at Galesburg, Illinois, on “Mr James Mather with whom I was acquainted in Utah, South Weber. He is comfortably situated, but has no religious tendencies remaining” (Forscutt, journal, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). Whether the Galesburg man is the roll’s James Mather is not settled; Family Tree’s James Mather (KWJJ-BBK) died in Iowa in 1898.

name: Laird, James
text: Summoned with Morris, the Cooks and Parson before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 28). Norma Allred’s compilation of South Weber households lists a James Laird, born in New York in 1832, son of John Laird, married to Cathrine Smith, daughter of Daniel Smith, and calls him “a polygamist and Morrisite”; his plural wife Mary Bright refused to go with him when he left South Weber after the war (Allred, South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952, 2004, no. 159 and Attachment 3). Catherine and Mary Laird follow him on the roll. Absent when the names of those bound over were called at the March 1863 term; his recognizance was declared forfeited ( Deseret News , March 18, 1863, p. 8).

name: Laird, Mary
text: Probably Mary Bright (born 1843 in England), daughter of John Bright and Sarah Webb, and a plural wife of James Laird. South Weber tradition, as compiled by Norma Allred, says she lived in a log cabin near the mountains from about 1858 to 1862, refused to go with Laird when he left South Weber after the war, and married Thomas Henry Peek in 1864 (Allred, South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952, 2004, nos. 5 and 159). Not checked against Family Tree.

name: Klingbeck, Solsan F.
text: Probably Johan Frederik Fransen Klingbaek (1815–1885), brother of Jacob Carl Klingbech, whose journal survives at the Church History Library; “Solsan” reads as a misprint for Johan. Born June 8, 1815, at Gudum, Denmark, he was a Latter-day Saint conference president in Denmark until February 1859 and came to Utah that year. By his journal, he heard in 1861 of a man north of Salt Lake City said to be the seventh angel, prayed about him, and left with his family on July 8, 1861, reaching South Weber on July 13. He and his second wife, Karen Andersen (roll: Karen), were baptized on July 21, and on July 22 Morris ordained him to the high priesthood. He was the “John Fred. Klingbeck” named Lieutenant at Arms of the First Division of the Soldiers of Israel on May 16, 1862. After the surrender he lived at Farmington, Utah, and wrote of himself as a stranger on the earth with the prophet dead. On March 25, 1869, he and his son Erastus were baptized into the Reorganized Church by E. C. Brand and enrolled in the Mottsville branch in Nevada's Carson Valley; W. W. Blair ordained him an elder at a conference at Carson City on November 13, 1869, with authority to preach in Idaho, Utah and Montana. From 1870 he lived among Danes in the Payette Valley, Idaho, where on May 23, 1872, he baptized his brother Jacob Carl. The Reorganized Church’s Danish Mission Fund lists a gift on December 17, 1874, from “J. F. Clengbak, Idaho” ( Saints’ Herald 22, 1875, p. 94). He died at Emmett, Idaho, on Apri

name: Klingbeck, Karen
text: Probably Karen Andersen (1839–1861), born July 1, 1839, on Als, Denmark, second wife of Johan F. F. Klingbaek (roll: Solsan F.). By his journal, they came to South Weber on July 13, 1861, and were baptized on July 21. Their daughter, born there on August 17, 1861, died two hours after birth. Karen fell ill after a visit to Salt Lake City; on October 3 Morris laid his hands on her, and she died at South Weber on October 19, 1861 (Johan F. F. Klingbaek journal, circa 1857–1877, MS 8268, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Forscutt, Elizabeth
text: Elizabeth Unsworth (1835–1903; FamilySearch L7NR-6JW), wife of Mark Hill Forscutt. By her obituary in the Saints’ Herald she was born at Bolton, England, on December 25, 1835, and “in early childhood joined the Church”; she married Forscutt in March 1860 and crossed to Utah that year with a handcart company (the obituary prints “1868”). It says she “never united with the Utah Church,” though she is on the Morrisite roll, and that she followed her husband to the States two years after he was “compelled to leave” Utah in 1866. From 1876 she kept a millinery business at Nebraska City, where she died of bronchial trouble on October 5, 1903, thirteen days before her husband; her children were Amy (Mrs. Parr), Ruby (Mrs. Lee Faunce) and Zenos. Frederick M. Smith preached at her funeral. The obituary appeared in the RLDS paper, but no record of her baptism into the Reorganized Church or reception into it has been found ( Saints’ Herald 50, 1903, p. 998).

name: Hastings, Winter
text: Winter Hastings (1831–1915), born in Yorkshire, came to Utah about 1860 and was excommunicated with Mary Hastings at Slaterville as a follower of Morris on March 31, 1861 (Holley, UHQ 76, 2008, p. 253 n.). A captain in the Second Division, he was discharged at Kington Fort on June 16, 1862, and later said he had seen Morris shot (Young, Contributor 11, 1890, pp. 283–84; CR 100 397; Saints’ Herald 38, 1891, p. 134). He lived in California and then at Springfield, Illinois, where he was active among spiritualists in 1875, joined the Reorganized Church in Washington in 1891, and died at its home for the aged at Lamoni in 1915 (1870 census; Religio-Philosophical Journal 18, 1875, p. 124; Saints’ Herald 62, 1915, p. 1165).

name: Willadson, Soren
text: ## Denmark and Iowa, 1816–60 In Denmark he was Søren Willadsen or Villadsen, son of Willads and Marin Sørensen, and he married Ane Margrethe Jensdatter (the roll’s Anne M.) on November 9, 1845. The “Soren Wilson” whose obituary is in the Saints’ Herald : born October 28, 1816, at Østrup, Saltum parish, Denmark, he joined the Latter-day Saints there and was ordained an elder; he came to America with his family in 1857 and lived near Burlington, Iowa, until 1860, when he went on to Salt Lake City. The emigration register confirms the identification: “Soren Willardson,” 40, a labourer from Jutland, crossed from Liverpool to Philadelphia from May 30 to July 3, 1857, with Anna Margreta, 36, Elsa Marie, 9, Maren, 6, Jens, 4, and Christen, 3, an infant Elisabet and Joseph Smith, 1, recorded under Wilhelmsen, Willardsen and Willardson; Anna Margreta, Elsa Marie, Maren and Christen are the roll’s Anne M., Else Maria, Maren and Christian Willadson (Saints by Sea, BYU, passenger record 61029, from the Scandinavian Mission emigration records, BMR p. 77). Wilson is a common anglicizing of Villadsen. ## Utah, California and the Reorganized Church, 1860–91 He “joined the Morrisites; became discouraged and went to California, thence back to Burlington, Iowa,” where he and his family were baptized into the Reorganized Church in the spring of 1876 by Mark H. Forscutt, who also ordained him an elder. A family history written by a great-granddaughter, given on the memorial, says that in Utah chu

name: Chase, Mahlon
text: Probably the “Bro. Mahlon Chase” whose wife Phoebe Chase, aged 35, died at Reese Creek, Montana, on September 27, 1887; Elder Gomer Reese of the Reorganized Church conducted the funeral ( Saints’ Herald 34, 1887, p. 759). Phoebe, born about 1852, was a later wife. The notice suggests an RLDS household, but not that he was himself a member.

name: Willadson, Anne M.
text: Ane Margrethe Jensdatter (1820–1898), wife of Søren Willadsen (the roll’s Soren Willadson) from November 9, 1845; born October 1, 1820, in Denmark. She is the “Anna Margreta,” 36, who crossed with him from Liverpool to Philadelphia in May–July 1857 (Saints by Sea, BYU, passenger records of the 1857 voyage, BMR p. 77). The family took the name Wilson. Her husband’s obituary says that “himself and family” were baptized into the Reorganized Church near Burlington, Iowa, in the spring of 1876 by Mark H. Forscutt. Her own obituary in the RLDS Saints’ Herald calls her “Sr. Anna Margret Jensen Wilson”: she died at Burlington on April 13, 1898, aged 77 years, 6 months and 13 days, and Elder J. S. Roth preached her funeral sermon on the 17th “at the Union church, nine miles west of Burlington” ( Saints’ Herald 45, April 27, 1898, p. 272). She is buried in Shiloh (Avery) Cemetery, Union Township, Des Moines County, beside her husband; the cemetery reading and her Find a Grave memorial give her death as April 30 (Find a Grave memorial 28063985).

name: Bryne, Catherine
text: Catherine Cardon (1829–1902; FamilySearch KPSD-PCZ), wife of Moses Byrne from November 5, 1854, when they married in Salt Lake City. The 1860 U.S. census gives her age as 30 and her birthplace as Italy, in Moses Byrne’s household at Ogden post office, Weber County, with their sons Joseph, John P. and James B. They had thirteen children, born 1855–73 (Family Tree). She was one of the Italian Piedmontese Cardons: Val Holley names “Slaterville’s Catherine Cardon Byrne and Marriott’s John Cardon” as brother and sister, the link between the Slaterville and Marriott Morrisites (Val Holley, “Slouching Towards Slaterville: Joseph Morris’s Wide Swath in Weber County,” Utah Historical Quarterly 76, no. 3 (Summer 2008): 250). The Slaterville Branch excommunicated her with Moses on March 31, 1861 (Holley, 253 n., from the Slaterville Ward Record of Members, Church History Library). Her brother is the roll’s John Cordon. Her sister Marie married Charles Guild, who ran the stage stop at Piedmont, Wyoming, where Catherine lived with Moses (“Piedmont Charcoal Kilns,” MS 351, Stewart Library, Weber State University).

name: Bryne, Ann
text: Anne Beus (1838–1905; FamilySearch KWNJ-JZK), plural wife of Moses Byrne from December 10, 1857, when they married in Salt Lake City (Family Tree). The 1860 U.S. census lists “Ann Byrne,” 20, born in Italy, with $100 in real estate and $30 in personal property, heading her own household at Ogden post office, Weber County, next door to Moses and Catherine Byrne, with a son of one year. Family Tree gives her seven children, born 1858–76. Holley notes that she was not on the Slaterville Branch’s excommunication list of 1861, though she is on the Morrisite roll (Val Holley, “Slouching Towards Slaterville: Joseph Morris’s Wide Swath in Weber County,” Utah Historical Quarterly 76, no. 3 (Summer 2008): 253 n.).

name: Cordon, John
text: Probably John (Jean) Cardon of Marriott, brother of Catherine Cardon Byrne (the roll’s Catherine Bryne): Val Holley names “Slaterville’s Catherine Cardon Byrne and Marriott’s John Cardon” as the Italian Piedmontese siblings who connected the Slaterville and Marriott Morrisites (Val Holley, “Slouching Towards Slaterville: Joseph Morris’s Wide Swath in Weber County,” Utah Historical Quarterly 76, no. 3 (Summer 2008)). The Church History Biographical Database has a Jean Cardon (1824–1909), a Waldensian, in the Robert L. Campbell company of 1854, the year Catherine came to Utah; that he is the same man has not been checked against Family Tree.

name: Willadson, Else Maria
text: Elsie Eliza Mary Hoverson (1847–1914), “daughter of Soren Wilson” (the roll’s Soren Willadson ), born in Denmark on April 15, 1847; she came to the United States at ten, with her parents in 1857. She married Andrew A. Hoverson at San Francisco on June 11, 1865, which places the family in California after the Morrisite years, and died near Burlington, Iowa, on July 26, 1914. Her obituary names among her survivors her sisters Anna and Sarah Wilson, who lived near her, Mrs. Eva Thomas of Burlington and Mrs. Mary Anderson of Lamoni, and her brother Chris Wilson, of Lamoni; she was buried at the Shiloh church cemetery ( Saints’ Herald 61, 1914, p. 847).

name: Willadson, Christian
text: Probably the “Chris Wilson, Lamoni” named in 1914 as the only surviving brother of Elsie Hoverson, the roll’s Else Maria Willadson ( Saints’ Herald 61, 1914, p. 847). The family took the name Wilson; the Christen who crossed with Soren Willadson in 1857 (Saints by Sea, passenger records of the 1857 voyage) is probably he.

name: Richards, David
text: A David Richards interpreted “The Testimony of the Third Captain of the Lord’s Host,” given in a tongue through Joseph Morris at Weber on June 8, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, pp. 638–42); probably the David Richards of the roll, who was in the First Division, No. 3 Company, but the name is common.

name: Larsen, Lars Christian
text: Probably Lars Christian Larsen (1833–1909; FamilySearch L41L-SWK), who came to Utah in 1859 and died at Deer Lodge, Montana. He was probably the L. C. Larsen with whom Sven Olson Hagg spent the winter of 1865–66 in the Deer Lodge Valley, and whose new house, which Hagg helped build, served for the Morrisites’ meetings (Hagg to A. Hanssen, March 4, 1866, Church History Library, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). The land office’s ledger of claims, its tract book, records that a Lars C. Larsen claimed 157 acres in the valley as a settler in 1869 and bought them for $196.44, at $1.25 an acre, on May 26, 1870 (Bureau of Land Management tract book, Montana, vol. 5, p. 96, township 8 north, range 9 west; images on FamilySearch, “United States, Bureau of Land Management Tract Books”). In 1880 he was living at Cottonwood Creek, Deer Lodge County (1880 U.S. census).

name: Morris, Joseph
text: The prophet himself. The printed roll lists his followers, not Morris. His wife Mary Olsen, a Danish convert he married soon after a revelation of August 23, 1861, is probably the roll’s “Mary Morris”; she was probably Karen Marie Olsen (born 1843), daughter of Ole and Anne Olsen, and so probably also the roll’s “Karen Morris” (see the roll notes for Karen Morris and Mary Morris). In 1878 James Bowman, at Soda Springs, mentions a debt of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law,” apparently living nearby; he is not named (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). Born at Burwardsley, Cheshire, he was a coal miner as a boy at Dukinfield and married Mary Thorp, a weaver, at Mottram in Longdendale in February 1847; three of their children died in infancy, in Cheshire and at St. Louis, and a daughter, Ann Eliza, was born on the trail in September 1853. In April 1854 Morris petitioned the Sanpete probate court for a divorce; Mary married Henry Beal at Ephraim in July and raised Ann Eliza (later Mrs. Alfred Pehrson, 1853–1939) in the Beal household. Mary Thorpe Beal died at Ephraim in 1905; she was the grandmother of Thorpe B. Isaacson, a counselor in the First Presidency. Morris’s second and third marriages, to the widow Elizabeth Mills (1855) and to Elizabeth Jones at Provo (1857), were short. His elder brother George’s reminiscences give his life before Utah (see Documents), and the Chronology gives the records. (Anderson, Revisited , 87, 104–5; The Spirit Prevails , 149–51; George Morris reminiscences, CHL MS 1614, 115–22; Mottram in Longdendale marriage register, 1847; 1841 and 1850 censuses; Merrill D. Beal, 1971, 35; Utah death certificates, 1905, 1939)

name: Aggerson, Hans
text: Fined $100 for resisting an officer at the March 1863 term; probably the “H. Okensen” held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Edwards, John C.
text: Held to bail as “J. C. Edwards” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Halse, Samuel
text: Held to bail as “Saml. Hulse” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Moffat, Peter
text: Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Neilsen, Kadrup
text: Convicted of murder in the second degree in March 1863 and sentenced to ten years at hard labor; pardoned by Governor Harding. (Deseret News , April 1, 1863)

name: Parr, L.
text: Held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862)

name: Peterson, James
text: Fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , April 1, 1863)

name: Rasmussen, Soren Peter
text: Held to bail as “S. P. Rasmusson” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Reese, John E.
text: A Welshman in No. 3 Company of the Soldiers of Israel (May 1862), named by W. P. Thomas among the Welsh at Kington Fort on Foreshadowing Day; taken prisoner at the surrender (“South Wales, 44”), held to bail as “J. E. Reese,” fined $100 for resisting an officer and pardoned in March 1863. Very probably, and by his family’s tradition, the John E. Reese who settled in the Gallatin Valley, Montana, and led the Reorganized Church there for most of 1869–1900, baptizing the Morrisites Anders and Katie Christoffersen in 1870. See his page . (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863; W. P. Thomas, letter of May 30, 1862, MS 31876, folder 21; translation generated by Claude; Young, Contributor 11 (1890): 283–84; CR 100 397; Saints’ Herald 47 (1900): 236)

name: Howels, Rees
text: A Welshman at Kington Fort on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862, named by W. P. Thomas with John E. Rees, David Powell and W. W. Thomas as sending remembrances to relatives in Wales. (W. P. Thomas, letter of May 30, 1862, MS 31876, folder 21; translation generated by Claude)

name: Morris, John
text: A Welshman at Kington Fort who helped W. P. Thomas plait the mane of Joseph Morris’s horse into seven skeins with white ribbons on the morning of Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862. No relation to the prophet is stated. (W. P. Thomas, letter of May 30, 1862, MS 31876, folder 21; translation generated by Claude)

name: Sorenson, John Peter
text: Held to bail as “J. P. Sorensen” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Williamsen, S.
text: Held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862)

name: Williams, George
text: The “Prophet Cainan,” who claimed to be Morris’s successor and led the church that regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s; in January 1879 he wrote that the Montana Saints lived on “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming (see the Chronology). (Anderson, Revisited ; Watson)

name: Hendrikson, Andrew
text: A Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint, born at Ondrup, Jutland, on July 29, 1843, and baptized into the Morrisite church in the Missouri River at Omaha on January 22, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871,” Council Bluffs, MS 32226). Williams named him “the Keeper of the Book” for the Omaha and Council Bluffs fund in October 1869, and he baptized converts in Nebraska and Iowa in 1870–71. In 1872 he went to the Deer Lodge Valley, married Carrie Jensen and was made second counselor to William James; in 1878 the council chose his land at Race Track for the Lord’s House (Church History Library, MS 31876). Counselor to James from May 1882, he presided over the Montana church from 1886 until his death in 1921; his records, kept by his family, are a main source for Anderson’s book. His family, the 1880 fire that killed a young daughter, and his later years are on his page . (Anderson, Revisited)

name: Johnson, George
text: Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty years, likewise never a Latter-day Saint; presided at the Lord’s House near Racetrack from 1921 until shortly before his death at ninety-eight, the last official leader of the Montana church. A county biography of about 1902 says he came to Montana in the summer of 1873, worked in Deer Lodge hotels, and then took up a stock ranch eight miles south of the town, and that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” On July 1, 1876, he married Josephine V. Oleson, a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. (Anderson, Revisited ; Progressive Men of the State of Montana (Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902]), pp. 1092–93)

name: Beck, Lars P.
text: Lars Peter Beck. Born in Jylland (Jutland), Denmark; came to America in 1864 and married Maria Christensen at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, on March 7, 1869. Baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, on August 20, 1871, by Andrew Henriksen and Niels Jensen, with his wife Maria; their eldest daughter had been born at Fremont in 1870. Ordained a Seventy in Montana on November 10, 1872, and a member of the council of the Danish-speaking stake from 1873 to 1883; the council met in his house near Deer Lodge on February 21, 1875, and their daughter Margaret was born at Deer Lodge that May. With his brother Nels J. Beck he met William P. Thomas at the Deer Lodge courthouse in 1880. In February 1883 he said he could not see that choosing a president would do the church any good, and he was among the minority who would not accept William James’s election that April; his brother Nels voted for James. On May 26, 1883, the Race Track council released him as a teacher and, with his wife, from membership, saying that the dissenters “had separated themselves from us” (minutes, MS 31876, Minutes, 1883–1884; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Their children included Annie, Mary Ann, Margaret, Laura, Carl R., Harry H. and Joseph. He died at Deer Lodge on February 21, 1925, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery there. (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), and minutebooks, 1872–1874, p. 3, and 1881–1890, pp. 10–11, MS 32226, Church History Library; council minutes, 1873–1883, MS 31876, Church History Library (translations from the Danish generated by Claude); Find a Grave 67303646; FamilySearch Family Tree, LK44-Y7K; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

name: Beck, Maria
text: Born in Slesvig (Schleswig), on January 7, 1847. Married Lars P. Beck (above) at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, in 1869, and was baptized with him at Fremont, Nebraska, on August 20, 1871, by Niels Jensen and Andrew Henriksen; the family settled near Deer Lodge, Montana, by 1875. Her maiden name was Christensen (Christiansen on her Find a Grave memorial). She died on May 13, 1938, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge. (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library (translation from the Danish generated by Claude); Find a Grave 67303647; FamilySearch Family Tree, L4QB-7GT; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

name: Beck, Nels J.
text: Nels Jensen Beck, brother of Lars P. Beck (above). Born at Jernved, near Ribe, Denmark, on May 6, 1847; came to America in 1872 and married Marie Helen Hansen at Deer Lodge that year; lived on Cottonwood Creek. The Montana council minutes of May 29, 1880, name “Lars Beck” and “his brother Niels Beck.” At the general assembly of April 25, 1883, “Nels Beck” and his wife voted to sustain William James, while Lars voted against. On April 25, 1887, “N. J. Beck” was made one of the three trustees of the Lord’s House, with George Johnson and Emmanuel Strome, so that the building would not be taxed. Other “Niels Beck” entries in the minutes may be he or the roll’s Niels R. Beck. He died on October 4, 1921, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge. (Council minutes, May 29, 1880, MS 31876, and elections and court, 1886–87, MS 31876, Church History Library; minutebook, 1881–1890, pp. 10–11, MS 32226, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, GB7W-C7D; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

name: Strom, Emanuel
text: In a note in his record book he gives his birth year as 1846 and says he was received into “the church of the Saints of the Most High God” at Omaha, Nebraska, in 1872 (day and month uncertain; translation from the Swedish generated by Claude). That year he copied Williams’s epistles and Morris’s revelations into Swedish. In March 1887, when Eardley went east, “Brother Strom” was to conduct the meetings, and on April 25, 1887, “Emmanuel Strome” was made one of the three trustees of the Lord’s House. In 1924 he wrote, and signed “E Strom,” that a feeling had explained to him “the League of Nation, to be united and ready when the Lord want them,” and that a voice had said “1926 Salt Lake City shall be destroid and laid waist.” He sat on the Race Track council in 1876 and 1880. In January 1880, after a visiting preacher named Brand had spoken in the Lord’s House, he said that no “sectarian” preacher should speak there; in May he put to the council a question about Adam and Eve and the serpent, and was asked to bring his violin to the Fourth of July at Deer Lodge. In May 1881 he would not take the sacrament from Erik Eliason, who he said “had come forward and set himself in Cainan’s place and would not take counsel” (translations from the Danish generated by Claude). On February 20, 1880, at Lower Warm Spring Creek, he married Mary Josephine Hellstrom, daughter of Johan Helström (below). He died on January 2, 1929, and is buried at Anaconda. (Record of epistles from Cainan, 1868–1872, and Record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, MS 31876, Church History Library; council minutes, 1876, 1880 and 1881, MS 31876, Church History Library; Eardley to Hendrikson, March 11 and 18, 1887, and elections and court, 1886–87, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, K4YW-8YS)

name: Helström, Johan
text: Very probably the “Johan Helström,” born May 1, 1834, in “Dalene” [Dalarna?], Sweden, whom the Omaha register lists as baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, on March 25, 1871, with Maria Helström. Family Tree has Johan Hellstrom born on April 29, 1834, at Gagnef, Dalarna; emigrated in 1864; died at Anaconda, Montana, on March 31, 1913. His daughter Mary Josephine married Emanuel Strom (above) in 1880. His son Peter Helstrom’s wife and children were to be baptized at Race Track on August 9, 1893. He sat on the Race Track council in 1876 and 1880. In 1876 the council heard a letter from Strom about his drinking, and in January 1880 it forgave him, after he had admitted being “under drink” and making threats over land, on condition that he give up strong drink “except the use of the wine at the Lord’s Supper” (translation from the Danish generated by Claude). A Peter E. Helstrom, very probably his son, was the elder in charge of the Reorganized Church’s Anaconda branch in 1926, when it had 42 members and no building (U.S. Census of Religious Bodies, 1926, schedule 489, American Religious Ecologies). (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), nos. 31–32, MS 32226, Church History Library; Eardley to Hendrikson, July 27, 1893, and council minutes, 1876 and 1880, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, KFR2-9KR)

name: Nielsen, Peter
text: Born at Aalborg, Jutland, Denmark, on February 27, 1833. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on June 26, 1870, by Rasmus Rasmussen and Andrew Hendrikson. He went to Montana, and on July 27, 1887, Joseph C. Clapp baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Deer Lodge, as “Peter Neilson,” with members of his family; the branch register marks him as since deceased. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 27 and no. 25)

name: Thorkelsen, Niels
text: Born at Lyby [?], Skåne, Sweden, on March 3, 1823. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on July 22, 1871, by Andrew Hendrikson and Jens Jensen, with Pernelle Tyrkelsen; the draft register notes that he moved to Montana. In October 1890 he was baptized into the Reorganized Church in the Deer Lodge Valley, entered as “Neil Tarkelson.” Family Tree has Niels Torgelson, born March 4, 1823, at Lyby, Malmöhus, Sweden, husband of Pernilla Bengtsson (1824–1891), who died at Anaconda, Montana, on June 9, 1913. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 37 and no. 61; FamilySearch Family Tree, K2HT-982)

name: Jensen, Niels
text: Born in Jutland, Denmark, on March 12, 1829. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on March 12, 1869, by Jens Jensen, and confirmed by S. P. Guhl; in 1869 he led the district at Florence under the Omaha congregation, and at Fremont in 1871 he baptized new members with Hendrikson. He kept a record book of Williams’s letters in Danish copies, 1870–79, which also holds a letter of 1875 from the claimant Barnet Moses Giles (see Repositories ). About March 1890 Joseph C. Clapp baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Willow Glen, Montana, with a Mary Jensen, born January 16, 1828, very probably his wife Maren, whom the Omaha register gives as born June 16, 1828. Family Tree has Niels Jensen, born March 12, 1829, at Smidstrup, Vejle, Denmark, married in 1851 to Maren Sørensdatter (1828–1914); he died at Deer Lodge, Montana, on November 22, 1914. The identification of the Montana Niels Jensen with the Omaha one rests on the matching birth date and wife. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 16 and nos. 59–60; Niels Jensen record, 1870–1879, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, KH45-1ZT)

name: Andrews
text: Foreman and agent of the community; Davies sent him east. A former member called him the “destroying angel”; another said he left of his own accord. Given name not recorded. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Bowman, Joseph
text: Called “the first born in the kingdom”; in Davies’s teaching he was counted among Davies’s sons, as Elias reincarnated. Compare Lewis H. Bowman, to whom Davies gave notes in 1879. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Cilley, Asa B.
text: A blacksmith from Stockton, California, who learned the doctrine at Portland, Oregon, in the winter of 1870–71 and came to the camp in November 1871. He left in June 1879 and sued Davies with Evans and Courtney; the court awarded him $125. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Clore, Jesse Y.
text: Born in Kentucky; first heard the doctrine at Gold Hill, Nevada, and took the vow at San Francisco about 1869. He lived at the camp, homesteaded four miles away, and testified for Davies in 1881 (“Jesse Y. Close” in the 1880 census). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census; The Sun (New York), November 14, 1878)

name: Corbett, Mrs. M. B.
text: On Davies’s list of members in March 1881, aged 47; “Mary Corbet” in the 1880 census. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Courtney, A. J.
text: At the camp from about 1876 to July 1877; a plaintiff against Davies, awarded $400. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Degroot, Mrs.
text: Credited with gifts of $218, 1869–78. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

name: Evans, Thomas W.
text: A plaintiff against Davies, awarded $2,700, the largest share. Davies said he came in 1870 and left in the spring of 1878. A Davies letter of March 1877 to a T. B. Evans, who was blind, looked for him “to come with Mr. Livingstone,” the roll’s R. J. Livingston of Carson Valley. Emma Evans also testified. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Hagg, Ola
text: Born in Sweden; at the camp from July 1868, and a witness for Davies in 1881. Probably the father of the roll’s Svend Hegg (Sven Olasson). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Hollenbeck, Mrs.
text: Credited with gifts of $195, 1869–74. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

name: Jones, Rachel D.
text: Mrs. John E. Jones, born in Wales; a member from 1866, she came to Walla Walla with Davies in 1867. Her children were born in Utah and Montana. Her husband, sent out as a missionary in 1868 and later at Indian Valley, may be the roll’s apostle John E. Jones; that is not settled. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Kelley, Michael H.
text: A sailor, born in Ireland; first came to the camp in November 1868, having learned the doctrine at San Francisco. Testified for Davies in 1881. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Lambert, V. D.
text: A cooper and later a justice of the peace; Davies’s missionary at San Francisco in 1869–70. He left the community and testified against Davies. Sarah Lambert also testified. The Walla Walla Statesman printed his testimony as “D. V. Lambert”: fifty-two, a cooper and a justice of the peace, who had known Davies since 1868 through his missionaries Robert Roberts and Thomas Parker at San Francisco, and whom Davies ordained a preacher (February 5, 1881, p. 3). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Miller, Søren
text: “Sorn Miller,” born in Denmark, at the camp from July 1868 with his wife and children Christian J., John M. and Christina, who are all on Davies’s 1881 list. Klemgard’s testimony implies that the elder Miller had been with him in Utah or at Soda Springs, that is, among the Morrisites. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Mortensen, James
text: “J. Mortezen,” a shoemaker born in Sweden, at the camp from July 1868 with his wife Maria; their daughter Maria and Oscar Olsen are on the 1881 list. Whether the family connects to the Mortensens on the roll is not known. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Parker, Mrs. E. S. J.
text: A widow, a member from 1868, at San Francisco. Probably the widow of Thomas Parker, Davies’s missionary there; whether he is the Thomas Parker on the roll is not settled. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Parker, Mary B.
text: “Mrs. Parker of San Francisco,” credited with gifts of $2,363.40, 1868–77. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

name: Perkins, Cornelia S.
text: Born in New Hampshire; a member from 1869 at San Francisco, at the camp from that fall. She took the minutes of meetings in shorthand, helped print the community’s tracts and taught the district school; later Davies’s second wife. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census; Find a Grave)

name: Perkins, M. A. C.
text: Cornelia’s mother, a member from 1869 at San Francisco, at the camp from 1872. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Roberts, Jane S.
text: Born in England; at the camp from 1868, with her daughter Emily J. Roberts. Testified for Davies in 1881. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Roberts, Robert
text: Husband of Jane S. Roberts; Davies’s missionary at San Francisco and Portland, who preached the doctrine and administered the vow. Almost certainly the “old man Robert Roberts” who visited Genoa, Nevada, in June 1876 claiming to be the Prophet Daniel, told the town that the child who was to “run” the Kingdom of God was born at Walla Walla, and addressed a Morrisite meeting in the court house; the paper called him “the Morrisite Mormon who claims to be the Prophet Daniel” when he came again in June 1877. He was later expelled from the community and did not return. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; Carson Valley News , June 23, 1876, May 29 and June 22, 1877)

name: Smith, Mrs.
text: Credited with gifts of $122. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

name: Turnbull
text: Named with Robert Roberts as administering the vow at San Francisco about 1869. Given name not recorded. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

name: Wood, S. W.
text: A photographer, born in England, who had an upholstery shop in Portland; he heard of Davies at San Francisco in 1868, came to the camp in the fall of 1869, served as a missionary and is credited with $5,921.65 on the list of donations. A defendant in the 1880 suit (“Samuel Woods” in the 1880 census). In November 1878 he passed through New York on his way to England to proclaim that the Messiah had come, and told the Sun of Davies’s revelation in Montana in 1866 and of the “Redemptionists” ( The Sun (New York), November 14, 1878, p. 1). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

name: Bowman, Isabella
text: Killed at Kington Fort during the surrender, one of the two women shot by Robert T. Burton’s party. Burton was indicted for her killing in 1870 (the indictment was voided in 1872) and again in 1877, tried from February 18, 1879, and acquitted. Alexander Dow’s affidavit of April 1863 calls her “Mrs. Bowman, wife of James Bowman.” The 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letter says she was holding Joseph March’s baby, whom she had taken in after its mother was killed. Wife of James Bowman (below), who was still a believer at Soda Springs in 1878. Not on the printed roll; she may have joined after it was made. South Weber City’s cemetery records say that “Bella Bowman” was buried outside the Pioneer Cemetery fence near its northeast corner. (Salt Lake Herald and Salt Lake Weekly Tribune , Feb.–Mar. 1879 (Burton trial); Salt Lake Tribune , July 26, 1891; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman); Anderson, Revisited , 148–49; South Weber City cemetery records)

name: Bowman, James
text: Husband of Isabella Bowman, who was killed at the surrender. Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863; moved to Idaho in the spring of 1863. In 1879 he testified at Burton’s trial that he had lived at Soda Springs since 1863. In August 1878 he wrote from Soda Springs to Erick Eliason in Montana, signing himself “yours truly in the New Covenant”; he had received “the Epistle so kindly sent me by the friends in Deer Lodge” and passed it on to “Father Christofferson,” and among debts owed him he lists one of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). Not the John Bowman of the roll, who was at Kaysville in 1870 and South Weber in 1880; Anderson also treats them as two men. Norma Allred’s compilation of South Weber households lists “James & Sarah A.” Bowman in a log house there in 1860 and says that Sarah died in the cannon attack of June 13, 1862 (Norma Earl Allred, comp., South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952 (2004), no. 44); the name and the manner of death differ from the contemporary accounts of Isabella Bowman, and the compilation gives no source for them. He died at Soda Springs on June 7, 1903. The RLDS Saints’ Herald printed his death as that of “Elder James Bowman,” born February 19, 1816, at Manchester, England, with a tribute from the Soda Springs Idanha Chieftain : “No man in need who asked of him but received assistance.” The title suggests that he had joined th (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863; Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 21, 1879; Anderson, Revisited , 148, 162; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman); Saints’ Herald 51 (1904): 213; Saints’ Herald 22, December 1, 1875, p. 705)

name: Søndermark, Anders
text: Born at Vrensted, Jylland, Denmark, January 9, 1821; entered in the draft register as Anders Sørensen, an Aaronic priest. Baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, “by Morrisen og Mikkelsen,” very probably Niels Morrisen and Jens Mikkelsen (a Niels Morrison was among Morris’s followers at South Weber in February 1861), and confirmed by Joseph Morris; a member of the Omaha congregation from 1869, and probably the “Bro. Søndermark” of the Fremont council of November 30, 1871, who said he believed “J. Morris was a Prophet.” Excluded from the Omaha congregation on November 30, 1871. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude; Fremont council minutes, November 30, 1871, MS 31876; Wilford Woodruff journal, February 11, 1861, MS 1352)

name: Søndermark, Karen Sørensen
text: Born at Vrensted, Jylland, Denmark, October 9, 1822; entered in the draft register as Karen Maria Sørensen; wife of Anders Søndermark. Baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, “by Morrisen og Mikkelsen” (very probably Niels Morrisen and Jens Mikkelsen), and confirmed by Joseph Morris; a member of the Omaha congregation from 1869; excluded on November 30, 1871. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude)

name: Knudsen, Hans
text: Born on Fyn, Denmark. Baptized at South Weber on July 18, 1861, by Jens Mikkelsen and confirmed by Joseph Morris; a leading member of the Council Bluffs congregation from 1869, baptizing and confirming others there and at Omaha and Crescent City. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude)

name: Fellows, Carleton
text: Born at Buffalo, New York, August 15, 1809. Baptized at Omaha in 1869 by S. P. Guhl and Hans Knudsen; husband of “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” who had been baptized at South Weber. In 1869 Williams told him he had been Jonas, the father of Simon Peter. Both were excluded from the Council Bluffs congregation on February 5, 1871. In November 1876 his stepson S. P. Guhl baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Council Bluffs as “old Dr. Charleston Fallows, who has been through the chastening fire since the time the first Joseph preached in the region of Buffalo, N. Y. He has been in Utah, and through the Morrisite school.” (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude; record book, 1869, MS 31876; Saints’ Herald 23, December 15, 1876, p. 758)

name: Staffanson, Peter
text: A Swedish shoemaker from Skåne, born November 22, 1823, who joined the Latter-day Saints at Copenhagen in 1852, crossed on the James Nesmith in 1855 and lived at Brigham City, Utah, until the later 1860s. He was baptized into the Morrisite church at Crescent City, Iowa, on February 2, 1869, and presided there from 1870; with Andrew Hendrikson he baptized Carrie, Hendrikson’s future wife, in 1871. In Montana he was named to preside over the second quorum of Seventies in 1872, went over to William James’s English-speaking Stake No. 1 in 1878, and was its bishop by 1883; in 1886 he held with James against George Thompson. He died at his ranch on Lost Creek near Anaconda on June 16, 1913, and is buried in the family cemetery there. Two of his sons married daughters of Daniel James, and two grandsons married daughters of Hendrikson. His son Jacob and Jacob’s wife Glendora were baptized into the Reorganized Church at Anaconda by A. B. Moore on October 23, 1897 (Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District, #228, Community of Christ Library Archives, nos. 119, 124). See his page . (Council Bluffs record of members, 1869–71, and minutebooks, Church History Library, MS 32226 and MS 31876; Eardley to Hendrikson, May 2, 1886, MS 31876; Butte Daily Post , June 16, 1913, p. 8)

name: James, William M.
text: Also written William Morgan James. Life dates 1817–1903. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1872–1890. Where: Warm Spring Creek (Willow Glen); Stake No. 1. Role: President 1872; president of Stake No. 1; president of the church 1883–86; deposed 1886. Came by way of Nevada, sent by Eardley and Cainan (his own account, 1890). Sources: M72 (Sept 22, 1872); RM p. 1; CM 1881–90; 1880 census. Open question: Life dates from CHL catalog

name: James, Daniel
text: Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1872–1886. Where: Stake No. 1. Role: Bishop's counselor 1872; teacher; suspended 1886. Sources: M72; RM p. 1; CM Apr 25, 1883; May 10, 1886. Open question: Not on the roll under this name (the roll has a Reuben James)

name: James, Sister D.
text: Also written wife of Daniel James. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1886. Where: Stake No. 1. Sources: RM p. 1; CM Apr 25, 1886 (absent). Open question: Her given name

name: Thomas, William P.
text: Also written W. P. Thomas. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana by 1871–1880+. Where: Warm Springs Creek, east of where Anaconda was built. Role: Counselor to the president 1872; the church organized at his house, Sept 22, 1872; election judge at Gwendale, 1876. Came by way of Utah. Sources: M72; RM p. 1; land patents 1871 and 1880; New North-West, Mar 10, 1876 and Apr 30, 1880.

name: Thomas, Margaretta P.
text: Also written Margaret Thomas. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1872–1886. Where: Stake No. 1. Role: Reordained "Lady elect to preside over the Female Order," 1872. Sources: M72; RM p. 1; CM Apr 25, 1886 ("Sis. Thomas," absent).

name: Hendrikson, Andrew
text: Also written Hendrickson, Henrikson. Life dates 1843–1921. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1872–1921. Where: Race Track; Stake No. 2. Role: Counselor 1872; president of Stake No. 2; presided in Montana 1886–1921. Came by way of Omaha (baptized Jan 22, 1869). Sources: RM no. 1; M72; CM 1881–90; Others named. Open question: Also on Others named list

name: Hendrikson, Carie
text: Also written Karie; "Sister Henrickson". Life dates b. 1853. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1886. Where: Race Track. Came by way of Crescent City, Iowa (baptized Oct 16, 1871). Sources: RM no. 6; CM 1883, 1886 votes.

name: Hendrikson, Maryann
text: Also written Mary Ann. Life dates b. 1873. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1873–1886. Where: born at Warm Springs; Race Track. Came by way of born in Montana. Sources: RM no. 41; CM Apr 25, 1886 vote.

name: Hendrikson, Henry
text: Life dates b. 1877. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1877–1962. Where: born at Race Track. Came by way of born in Montana. Sources: RM no. 44; Cornelius thesis (1962 interview). Open question: Death date

name: Hendrikson, Jenny
text: Also written Jeny. Life dates b. 1878. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1878–1887. Where: born at Race Track. Came by way of born in Montana. Sources: RM no. 45.

name: Jensen, Jens
text: Life dates b. 1834. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1883. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Clerk of the Danish council minutes (1876); opposed James 1883. Came by way of Omaha (baptized Jan 22, 1869). Sources: RM no. 2; DM 1876; CM Apr 25, 1883.

name: Jensen, Jacobene Hansine
text: Life dates b. 1833. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874+. Where: Stake No. 2. Came by way of Omaha (baptized 1869). Sources: RM no. 5.

name: Jensen, Emma Wilhelmine
text: Life dates b. 1864. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1876–1883. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Opposed James 1883. Came by way of born in Copenhagen; baptized at Deer Lodge 1876. Sources: RM no. 26; CM Apr 25, 1883.

name: Rasmussen, Rasmus
text: Also written Rasmusson. Life dates b. 1830. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1872–1884. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Bishop 1872; bishop of Stake No. 2 until suspended 1883; kept the records. Came by way of Omaha. Sources: M72; RM no. 3; CM 1881–84.

name: Rasmussen, Mary
text: Life dates b. 1846. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874+. Where: Stake No. 2. Came by way of Omaha (baptized 1869). Sources: RM no. 4.

name: Jorgenson, Lars Chr.
text: Life dates 1817–by 1883. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1883. Where: Stake No. 2. Came by way of Crescent City, Iowa (baptized 1869). Sources: RM no. 7; CM Nov 10, 1883 ("the late").

name: Jorgensen, Mary
text: Also written Sister Jorgenson. Life dates b. 1823. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1886. Where: Stake No. 2. Came by way of Crescent City, Iowa (baptized 1869). Sources: RM no. 8; CM 1883, 1886 votes; Anderson 1981, p. 212. Open question: Very probably the "Mary Jergensen" whom Anderson names as guardian of Carrie Jensen, Andrew Hendrikson's bride, in 1872

name: Just, Peter A.
text: Also written P. Just. Life dates b. 1816. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1883. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Opposed James 1883. Came by way of Omaha (baptized 1869). Sources: RM no. 9; CM 1882, 1883. Open question: A son in Idaho, 1882

name: Peterson, Andrew
text: Life dates b. 1837. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1883. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Opposed James 1883. Came by way of Fremont, Nebraska (baptized 1871). Sources: RM no. 10; CM Apr 25, 1883.

name: Peterson, Margereth
text: Also written Sister Petersen. Life dates b. 1845. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1883. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Opposed James 1883. Came by way of Fremont, Nebraska (baptized 1871). Sources: RM no. 11; CM Apr 25, 1883.

name: Boberg, Erick
text: Life dates b. 1845. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1886. Role: Voted for Thompson by letter, 1886. Came by way of Fremont, Nebraska (baptized 1871). Sources: RM no. 12; CM Apr 25, 1886.

name: Boberg, Christine
text: Life dates b. 1811. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874+. Came by way of Fremont, Nebraska (baptized 1871). Sources: RM no. 13.

name: Beck, Lars P.
text: Also written L. P. Beck. Life dates 1844–1925. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1925. Where: Stake No. 2. Role: Opposed James 1883. Came by way of Fremont, Nebraska (baptized 1871). Sources: RM no. 14; CM Apr 25, 1883; Others named.

name: Beck, Maria
text: Also written Mary Beck. Life dates 1847–1938. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1874–1938. Where: Stake No. 2. Came by way of Fremont, Nebraska (baptized 1871). Sources: RM no. 15; Others named.

name: Beck, Nels J.
text: Also written Niels J. Beck. Life dates 1847–1921. Status: Member (record of members). In Montana 1872–1921. Where: Cottonwood Creek. Role: Sat in the court 1887 and 1889; a trustee of the Lord's House from Apr 25, 1887, with George Johnson and Emanuel Strom. Came by way of Denmark; married at Deer Lodge 1872; baptized there 1878. Sources: RM no. 30; CM 1883, 1886, 1887, 1889; Others named.

name: Beck, Mary Helene
